#5496. Democrats flipped 7 Senate seats in 2026 — Republicans held Kansas for 94 years

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Senate seats Democrats flipped in 2026 span seven states, from Kansas to Maine, ending Republican holds that in some cases lasted decades

The last time a Democrat had won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas was 1932. That streak ended in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. It also closed out a Republican hold on the seat that The New York Times put at 94 years.

Kansas was one of seven Senate seats Democrats flipped in 2026. Those wins gave the party control of the chamber, according to The New York Times. The seven states were Kansas, Texas, North Carolina, Maine, South Carolina, Ohio and Iowa. Republicans held each of those seats going into the vote.

In North Carolina, Republicans had held the seat for 18 years. Democrats last won a Senate seat in the state in 2008. Republicans then won five consecutive Senate elections there.

In Maine, the defeated incumbent was Susan Collins, a five-term Republican senator. Her loss ended 30 years of Republican tenure in the seat.

Ohio's seat returned to Democratic hands after an appointed Republican had held it on a temporary basis. The Times described the Iowa result as a "battleground shift." Democrats won there in an upset that secured their route to a Senate majority.

The Times did not report how long Republicans held the seats in Texas, South Carolina, Ohio and Iowa.

The national count was not complete when these results were reported. In a tally timestamped 10:16 p.m., The Associated Press had called 33 of the 35 Senate seats up for election. Democrats stood at 54 seats in that count. The figure combined 20 races won, two races in which Democrats were leading and 34 seats carried over. It also included independents who caucus with Democrats.

Republicans stood at 44 seats in the same AP count. That total came from 13 races won and 31 seats carried over. The AP showed a gain of seven seats for Democrats and a loss of seven for Republicans.

Those totals were a snapshot, not a final result. The two races in which Democrats led had not been called. The 54 and 44 figures add up to 98 seats, leaving two of the Senate's 100 seats unaccounted for in that count.

A Democrat won a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. No Democrat had won a Kansas Senate seat since 1932.

The result ended 94 years of Republican control of the seat, according to The New York Times. That stretch is close to a century.

The Times based its results on its own reporting and on The Associated Press.

Kansas was one of seven Republican-held Senate seats that Democrats won in 2026. The Times gave tenure figures for three of those seats, in Kansas, North Carolina and Maine. Of the three, Kansas had the longest Republican hold.

Democrats took a U.S. Senate seat in Texas from Republicans in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. The New York Times listed Texas among the Republican-held seats that changed hands. The listing drew on results from the Times and The Associated Press.

That listing is the only published detail on the Texas race. The results do not say how long Republicans had held the seat.

They do not name the winning Democrat or the defeated Republican. They also give no margin of victory or vote share.

Democrats won a North Carolina U.S. Senate seat from Republicans in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. The New York Times reports that Republicans had held the seat for 18 years before the vote.

North Carolina was one of seven Republican-held Senate seats Democrats took that night, according to the Times. Together, those seven wins gave the party control of the chamber.

The result also broke a long Democratic losing streak in the state's Senate races. The party's last Senate win in North Carolina came in 2008.

Republicans then won five consecutive Senate elections in the state, the Times reports.

The 2026 result ended that run of Republican victories. It was the first Democratic Senate win in North Carolina since 2008.

Maine's U.S. Senate seat moved to the Democrats in the November 3, 2026 midterms when five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins lost. Her defeat ended 30 years of Republican tenure in the seat, according to The New York Times.

Collins was the sitting senator in the race. She lost the seat rather than leaving it open.

Maine was one of seven Republican-held Senate seats that Democrats won in the 2026 midterms. Together, those seats gave the party control of the chamber.

South Carolina was one of the seven U.S. Senate seats Democrats took from Republicans in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. The New York Times counted the state among the flips that handed Democrats control of the chamber.

The Times results for South Carolina go no further than the flip itself. They do not say how long Republicans had held the seat.

They also leave out the name of the winning Democrat and the defeated Republican. No vote share or margin of victory appears for the race.

Ohio's U.S. Senate seat went back to Democrats in the November 3, 2026 midterm elections. Going into the vote, the seat was held by a Republican who had been appointed to it on a temporary basis.

That sets Ohio apart from a typical flip. The Republican in the seat had reached the Senate through an appointment, not a statewide election. The midterm put the seat to Ohio voters, and a Democrat won it.

Ohio counted among the Republican-held seats Democrats flipped on their way to winning control of the Senate, according to The New York Times.

The Times gives no single figure for how long Republicans controlled the Ohio seat. Its tenure entry for the state reads only "varies by seat." It does not give a year when the Republican hold began.

The Times also labeled the Iowa race a "battleground shift."

Iowa was one of seven Republican-held Senate seats Democrats flipped in the 2026 midterms. The others were in Kansas, Texas, North Carolina, Maine, South Carolina and Ohio. The Times reported that those seven wins gave Democrats control of the chamber.

#5495. Rover hires Textio co-founder Jensen Harris and former Amazon exec Vik Rajagopal

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:07 am

Seattle-based pet care marketplace Rover is adding two executives to its leadership team: former Motus CFO Vik Rajagopal as chief financial officer and Textio co-founder Jensen Harris as president of marketplace, product and technology.

Rajagopal succeeds Charlie Wickers, who served as Rover’s CFO from 2022 to 2025. Harris succeeds Brent Turner, who was Rover’s president and chief operating officer before he was named CEO last year.

Rajagopal spent nearly a decade at Amazon, starting in 2011 as a finance lead for Amazon Global Selling, the program that helps sellers reach customers in other countries. He later became a general manager in Amazon’s retail business, running the U.S. shoes and luggage stores and the home store, as well as Amazon’s U.S. Vendor Success Program.

He left Amazon in late 2020 to become CFO of Logos, a maker of Bible study software backed by private equity firm Cove Hill Partners. He was promoted to CEO about a year later, replacing the company’s founder, and led Logos until April 2024. He was most recently CFO at Motus, which makes software that companies use to manage and reimburse employees who drive for work.

Earlier in his career, Rajagopal was an investment banker at Wells Fargo Securities and worked in corporate development at Symantec. He holds a bachelor’s degree from Yale and an MBA from Northwestern’s Kellogg School of Management.

“Rover is a Seattle company that was built the right way from day one — solving a real customer pain point with a strong product, solid economics, and a culture that is poised for long-term success,” Rajagopal said in a news release on Wednesday.

Harris co-founded Seattle-based Textio in 2014 with Kieran Snyder, his wife, after both worked on productivity software at Microsoft. The startup used AI to analyze workplace writing such as job posts and performance reviews. Harris was Textio’s CTO for nearly eight years, then chief experience officer, before taking over as CEO from Snyder in January 2024. He handed the CEO role to Colleen Gallagher in January 2026 and remains with Textio as founder emeritus.

Textio has raised $42.5 million from investors and went through rounds of layoffs in 2024 and 2025 under Harris. As CEO, he led the launch of Lavalier, an AI-based interview intelligence platform.

Before Textio, Harris spent more than 15 years at Microsoft, where he led the redesign of the Office user interface that produced the Ribbon, and later led user experience for Windows and the touch interface for the original Surface.

After leaving the CEO role at Textio, Harris founded Expedition 60, a firm that helps companies rework how they build software with AI.

“Our pets give us unconditional love, and they deserve the very best in return,” Harris said in a statement, adding that he shares a home with “three very opinionated cats.”

Rover was born at a 2011 Seattle Startup Weekend event, where venture capitalist Greg Gottesman pitched the idea. Aaron Easterly led the company as CEO for 14 years, taking it through the pandemic, a public offering and a $2.3 billion take-private deal with Blackstone in 2024. He stepped down last year and became executive chair, handing the CEO role to Turner.

Rover now operates in 18 countries across North America, Europe and Australia, and says sitters and walkers on its platform have provided 50 million bookings to date. Its brands include cat-sitting marketplaces Meowtel and Cat in a Flat, and Australia-based Mad Paws. Beyond sitting and walking, Rover now offers training in the U.S. and is testing other services.

#5494. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

Trump Media has moved $343 million in Bitcoin to Crypto.com, raising fresh questions if Donald Trump’s media company could be selling its crypto holdings. The transfer comes as Democrats prepare investigations into Trump’s family crypto ventures following their midterm election victories.

The timing is difficult to ignore. A sale has not been confirmed, but this move puts the company’s Bitcoin treasury under pressure.

Arkham data showed Trump Media-linked wallets transferring 4,259 BTC to Crypto.com just a few hours ago. The coins were moved in two batches of more than 2,000 BTC each. The transfer represents around $343 million at recent prices. It also accounts for 30% of the 14,139 BTC Trump Media previously held, including pledged coins.

However, the destination does not confirm a sale. It is known that Trump Media has used Crypto.com for custody and trading-related transfers before, including transactions in May and August.

The latest movement is particularly notable because the Bitcoin came from wallets associated with convertible-note collateral. Trump Media’s previous filings identified 4,260.73 BTC as collateral for its notes.

#5492. Nearly $12 billion in 2026 midterm spending, and 6 races that show it

Free daily briefing on global business news.

2026 midterm spending neared $12 billion, and these 7 big-money fights, from the Texas Senate race to three House contests past $50 million in ads, show where the cash went

Money is the easiest part of a campaign to count and one of the hardest to tie to a result. The 2026 midterms put that gap on full display. Total spending in the cycle reached nearly $12 billion. NPR described it as the most expensive U.S. election cycle yet, ahead of even the 2024 presidential race. The headline on that same NPR report offered a counterpoint: political ads aren't that effective.

That tension runs through this list. The record 2026 midterm spending did not flow evenly. NPR reported that most of it favored outside groups aligned with Republicans. Much of that outside money moves through super PACs. These groups can raise unlimited sums from individuals, corporations and unions as long as they do not coordinate directly with a candidate. That structure lets a single large donor shape a race in ways that capped contributions to a campaign cannot.

The money reached down the ballot as well. NPR reported that three House contests each passed $50 million in ad spending, the first time that had happened. All 435 House seats are on the ballot every two years. That puts control of the chamber up for a vote in every midterm.

The seven entries that follow are a selection, not a complete ranking. They cover the Senate races in Texas and Michigan, California's race for governor, House contests in North Carolina, New York and Florida, and the cycle as a whole. Each slide sets out who spent, how much where a figure is available, and where the money came from.

Whether the spending paid off is the harder question. Several reported outcomes could not be independently confirmed when this was written. Where a result is unconfirmed, the slides say so instead of guessing. Where reports give conflicting spending totals, the disputed figure is left out. What remains is a race-by-race record of where the money went. That record can be read against the argument in NPR's headline about the limits of political advertising.

Elon Musk put more than $150 million into super PACs backing Republican Ken Paxton in the 2026 Texas Senate race. Democrat James Talarico raised $145 million for his own campaign, mostly from smaller donors, while Paxton's campaign raised $22 million.

The contest matched two Texas officeholders. Paxton has served as the state's attorney general since 2015, after earlier terms in both chambers of the Texas Legislature. The Texas House impeached him in 2023, and the Texas Senate acquitted him later that year. Talarico, a former schoolteacher, has served in the Texas House of Representatives since 2019.

Total spending in the race ran well over $500 million. Published totals conflict, so no exact figure appears here.

The two sides paid for their campaigns in different ways. Most of the money working on Paxton's behalf came from outside groups, not from his own campaign. Musk's contributions alone came to more than six times what Paxton's campaign raised.

Talarico's money followed a different path. Contributions from smaller donors went directly to his campaign, which controlled how the money was spent. Counting candidate fundraising alone, Talarico raised $123 million more than Paxton.

Combined, Musk's super PAC money and Paxton's campaign fundraising came to more than $172 million. That sum exceeds Talarico's $145 million. It still covers only part of what was spent in the race.

The race also tested a long Republican hold on Texas Senate contests. Before 2026, Texas had last elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 1988, when Lloyd Bentsen won reelection. Bentsen was also the Democratic vice presidential nominee that year.

Reporting from NPR argues that political ads aren't that effective. Texas puts that argument to a direct test. One candidate relied mostly on smaller donors. His opponent had a single donor's nine-figure super PAC commitment behind him. The final result could not be confirmed from a dated report when this was written. This slide therefore does not name a winner or judge whether the money paid off.

Republicans outspent Democrats on general election advertising in Michigan's open Senate race, $143.5 million to $117 million, according to NPR. That gave the Republican side, backing Mike Rogers, a $26.5 million advantage over Democrats backing Abdul El-Sayed.

The Republican total was about 23% larger than the Democratic one. Combined, the two sides spent $260.5 million on general election ads in the state. Those figures cover the general election only. Money spent in either party's primary is not included.

The seat opened when Gary Peters, a Democrat first elected to it in 2014, announced in January 2025 that he would not seek a third term. Peters had served three terms in the U.S. House before moving to the Senate. His exit meant neither party had an incumbent on the ballot.

Rogers came into the race with a statewide campaign already behind him. He is a former Republican congressman from Michigan who chaired the House Intelligence Committee. In 2024, he ran for the state's other Senate seat and lost narrowly to Democrat Elissa Slotkin.

El-Sayed is a physician and epidemiologist who previously ran Detroit's health department. His first statewide bid came in 2018, when he ran for governor. He lost that Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer, who went on to win the office.

Both of Michigan's Senate seats were held by Democrats going into the 2026 cycle, by Peters and Slotkin. A Rogers win would give Republicans a pickup in a state that voted for Donald Trump in 2016, Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024.

No dated report confirming the outcome of the race was available when this was written. That leaves open the question of whether the spending paid off.

The result will still test the ad gap clearly. A Rogers victory would match the Republican advantage in general election ads. An El-Sayed victory would mean the side that spent $26.5 million less took the seat. That outcome would fit the argument in NPR's headline that political ads aren't that effective. One race cannot settle that question on its own.

California's governor's race drew $349.4 million in total spending, according to NPR. Most of that money went out during a crowded primary, before the field narrowed to two finalists for November.

NPR's reporting credits the primary spending with clearing out wildcard candidates. It says the result left the Democratic establishment in control of the race. That claim is the only point in the available reporting that speaks to whether the money paid off.

California's election rules give the primary unusual weight. The state uses a top-two primary, in which every candidate for governor appears on a single ballot regardless of party. The two candidates with the most votes advance to the general election, even if they belong to the same party.

Voters adopted the system by approving Proposition 14 in June 2010. It took effect with the 2012 elections. It covers state offices and congressional seats but not the presidential primary.

A same-party November matchup is possible under these rules. In 2016, two Democrats, Kamala Harris and Loretta Sanchez, faced each other in the general election for a U.S. Senate seat from California. No Republican appeared on that November ballot.

The previous open-seat race for governor followed a more familiar pattern. In 2018, Democrat Gavin Newsom and Republican John Cox finished first and second in the primary. Former Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa, also a Democrat, placed third and was eliminated. Newsom then won the general election.

The 2026 seat was open as well. Newsom was reelected in 2022, and California limits governors to two terms. Voters set that limit through Proposition 140 in 1990.

In a top-two system, a crowded field splits the vote among many candidates. A candidate needs only to finish second, not first, to reach November. Spending in that phase can decide which two names remain on the ballot.

The candidates' names and the eventual winner could not be confirmed when this was written. Neither could the split of the $349.4 million between campaigns and outside groups, or the vote results.

The race for North Carolina's 1st Congressional District, between Democrat Don Davis and Republican Laurie Buckhout, passed $50 million in ad spending, according to NPR. Davis has held the seat since January 2023, so the contest was a defense of a Democratic incumbent.

The $50 million mark counts advertising alone. Staff salaries, field operations, polling and other campaign costs fall outside it. The figure is a floor for ad spending in the district, not a full accounting of what campaigns and outside groups spent on the race.

No precise ad total for this district was available. Nor was a split of the money by party, candidate or outside group. The reporting also does not show which side bought more airtime.

Those gaps limit any verdict on whether the money paid off. A spending advantage can be weighed against a result only when it is clear which side held it. A dollar total also says nothing about how the ads ran, whether on broadcast television, cable or digital platforms.

The outcome could not be confirmed when this was written. No winner or vote margin for the district was available.

That leaves the race as an open test of NPR's argument that political ads have limited effect. A loss by the bigger spender would fit that argument. A win would not settle it. A district's partisan lean, the candidates and the national mood all shape how people vote. Ad money is only one input.

The House race between Republican Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley in New York's 17th District drew more than $50 million in ad spending, according to NPR. That total covers advertising alone, not the full cost of either campaign.

The district sits north of New York City in the lower Hudson Valley. It takes in all of Rockland and Putnam counties, along with parts of Westchester and Dutchess counties.

Lawler first won the seat in 2022. He defeated Democratic Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney, who chaired the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee at the time. Maloney had moved into the district after New York's 2022 redistricting. Two years later, Lawler held the seat against former Rep. Mondaire Jones. He entered the 2026 cycle as a two-term incumbent, with Conley as his Democratic challenger.

Joe Biden carried the district in the 2020 presidential election. That placed Lawler among the House Republicans representing seats Biden won.

The NPR figure is a combined total. It does not show how much each party, campaign or outside group spent. It also does not say whether one side outspent the other on the airwaves. Without that split, there is no basis for judging which campaign got more for its money.

The result could not be confirmed when this was written. No dated report naming a winner or giving a margin in this race was available. Whether the spending paid off for Lawler, for Conley or for the groups backing them cannot yet be judged.

The national pattern offers only partial context. NPR's coverage indicates that heavy ad spending yielded less and less for Republican challengers this cycle. Lawler was not a challenger in 2026. He was defending a seat he had already won twice. That national finding does not settle how ad money performed in this district.

What the record does show is scale. More than $50 million went to advertising in a single suburban House seat.

Florida's 25th District, where Jared Moskowitz faced Scott Singer, was one of three U.S. House contests in the 2026 midterms to pass $50 million in ad spending, according to NPR. The other two were North Carolina's 1st District and New York's 17th District.

The $50 million mark is a floor, not a final tally. NPR gives no exact ad spending figure for this district. The true total may be higher, and the available reporting does not say by how much.

The figure also counts advertising only. It leaves out other campaign costs, such as staff, field operations and voter outreach. The full cost of the contest is therefore larger than the ad figure by itself.

The reporting does not break the ad money down by spender, either. It does not say how much came from the Moskowitz campaign, the Singer campaign or outside groups such as super PACs. Without that split, there is no way to tell which candidate held the advertising edge. It also leaves open whether the candidates controlled most of the money or whether groups acting independently of them did.

The outcome is unconfirmed as well. The available material reports neither a winner nor a margin. No dated report confirming the result was available when this was written.

NPR's headline argues that political ads aren't that effective. Moskowitz vs. Singer cannot yet test that claim. For now, the race shows how high House ad budgets climbed in 2026, not whether the money moved votes. Settling that would take two records the reporting does not supply: a district-level breakdown of ad spending by side and a certified vote count.

Spending on the 2026 midterm cycle came close to $12 billion. In the fight for the House, NPR's report argues that the heavy ad spending bought less and less for Republican challengers.

That record came in a year with no presidential race on the ballot. Every federal contest in 2026 was for a seat in Congress.

The House was the main arena for testing what the money could buy. A party needs 218 seats to hold a majority. That puts every competitive district into the national count.

The phrase "less and less" describes diminishing returns. Read that way, each added round of advertising produced a smaller gain than the one before it. NPR's report does not say the spending had no effect on Republican challengers. It says the effect shrank as the money grew.

Challengers usually start with less name recognition than incumbents. Paid advertising is one of the main ways a campaign introduces a newcomer to voters. That makes Republican challengers a direct test of what ad dollars could and could not do.

NPR's report gives two reasons the money did not deliver more for them. It points to a national focus on affordability. It also says voters rejected the status quo.

Both explanations rest on issues and voter mood, not on the volume of advertising. Affordability is about costs voters meet in their own budgets. An ad can frame those costs, but it cannot change them. A rejection of the status quo is a judgment on current conditions. A campaign can argue about those conditions without controlling them. That reasoning lines up with NPR's case about the limits of political ads.

The same report says Democrats passed the 218-seat threshold and won the House majority. It also says Democrats won the Senate. A dated, independent report confirming either result was not available when this was written.

Whether the cycle's record spending paid off for either party depends on those final results. Until they are confirmed, the question stays open.

#5491. Finpilot raises $10M for AI agents that handle the grunt work for institutional investors

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 7:04 am

Seattle startup Finpilot, which uses AI agents to take the paperwork off the plates of people who invest money for hospitals, pension funds and foundations, has raised $10 million in a Series A round.

The round was led by Bay Area venture firm Lobby Capital, with participation from Madrona, which led Finpilot’s $4 million seed round in 2024. Finpilot, which has raised about $14.5 million since its 2023 founding, plans to use the new funding to expand its product and hire across the company.

Its customers include in-house investment teams at institutions and firms that manage money on their behalf. In the industry, they’re known as allocators, because they spread capital across outside fund managers. Much of their information arrives from fund managers as PDFs and spreadsheets, and someone has to read the reports, pull out the numbers and enter them into the right systems.

Finpilot pulls that information into one place and has its agents handle much of the work. The idea is to let investment teams spend their time on judgment and decisions, not on reading data from documents and typing it into a database, said Lakshay Chauhan, Finpilot’s co-founder and CEO, in an interview.

“Nobody wakes up like, ‘All right, I’m excited to do that,'” he said.

It’s a change of course for the company. When GeekWire covered its seed round, Finpilot was building a ChatGPT-style tool for analysts researching public companies. It shifted to allocators in mid-2024, Chauhan said, after concluding that AI added only marginal value in public markets, where Bloomberg and S&P Capital IQ had already organized most of the data.

“There’s no Bloomberg for what they do,” he said of allocators.

Customers include Seattle Children’s, Children’s Health in Dallas, Hackensack Meridian Health in New Jersey, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Wyoming, the Wyoming Retirement System, outsourced investment firm TIFF, and Seattle wealth management firm Laird Norton Wetherby. Some of those institutions hadn’t changed their core systems in 15 years, Chauhan said.

Finpilot has about 28 institutional customers in all, and revenue has grown tenfold since the start of the year, he said. It hasn’t lost a customer yet, he noted.

How it works: Finpilot pulls an institution’s data from its portfolio management system, document storage and other sources into a single record, matching each fund, holding and client to one identifier. Users ask questions in a chat window and set up agents to handle recurring work.

In an example Chauhan described, an agent could review updates from 35 private equity managers at the end of a quarter, figure out what changed and point an analyst to the three things that need attention. Agents also prepare briefings before meetings with fund managers, and they ask a person for approval when a step needs one.

Some customers run Finpilot alongside their existing software. Others have used it to replace older customer relationship management and research management systems, where investment teams log their dealings with fund managers.

Chauhan said Finpilot most often gets compared with general-purpose AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, including finance-focused versions like Claude for Financial Services, and with legacy CRM vendors.

Chauhan said the difference is accuracy. A 10-page report from a chatbot has to be checked number by number before it goes to a chief investment officer. In Finpilot, every number links back to the document it came from, so it can be checked.

In finance, he said, “you cannot be wrong.”

Finpilot runs its own in-house model for the high-volume job of reading financial documents, and uses models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google for other tasks. It doesn’t train AI models on customer data and keeps each customer’s data separate, Chauhan said.

Founders: Chauhan grew up in India and came to the U.S. for a master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He interned at Boeing in Seattle, but when he graduated, he said, many full-time aerospace jobs required U.S. citizenship or permanent residency, and he was in the country on a visa.

He went to work for an engineering optimization software company and studied quantitative investing on the side. That led him to a paper by John Alberg, co-founder of Seattle investment firm Euclidean Technologies, which uses machine learning to pick stocks. Chauhan called Alberg repeatedly to propose working together, and Alberg eventually hired him. Chauhan later led AI at Euclidean.

Alberg is Finpilot’s co-founder and executive chairman but isn’t involved in day-to-day operations. His late father, Tom Alberg, co-founded Madrona.

Finpilot has about 14 employees, up from four in 2024. All are based in Seattle except one in Boise, Idaho. The company recently moved into the AGC Building on Lake Union after outgrowing its old office.

What’s next: Finpilot plans to fill six or seven jobs in the next few months, in product, marketing, client success, sales and business development, and about as many early next year.

Part of the money will go to implementation teams, Chauhan said. Their job is to sit down with each customer, learn how its investment team works and show it how to redo that work with AI agents.

#5490. In-N-Out’s billionaire owner vows iconic chain ‘will always be’ in California and says leaving the state would be the ‘dumbest business decision ever’

Lynsi Snyder, president and owner of In-N-Out, moved her family to Tennessee recently but reaffirmed that the iconic burger chain will never abandon California.

In an interview with actor Terry Crews that In-N-Out posted online, she was asked how the company will retain its California DNA as it expands to more states around the country.

“This is where we started. It’s where we are now, and it’s where we will always be,” Snyder replied.

Her grandparents opened the first In-N-Out in Southern California in 1948, and the company has gradually expanded to other parts of the state—and to other parts of the country.

While far from being the biggest chain, it retains a cult following that has helped its expansion as people who moved out of California make pilgrimages when restaurants open in new states.

But Snyder, who grew up in Northern California, revealed last year that she and her family were moving to Tennessee, saying that raising kids was difficult in the state and that “doing business is not easy” there either.

That sparked fears In-N-Out might leave California, prompting the burger heiress—who is worth an estimated $7.3 billion—to clarify that her departure from the state doesn’t mean the company will too.

In a video posted to her Instagram page last year, Snyder told followers: “We’re not leaving California, or leaving our roots behind. Each one of our locations is here to stay.”

Still, there has been a corporate exodus from California to states like Texas, where Elon Musk has relocated the headquarters for Tesla and SpaceX.

In-N-Out has also clashed with state authorities, such as when it refused to comply with officials and request that customers must show proof of vaccination to make purchases during the pandemic.

And the company reluctantly raised prices after California imposed higher minimum wages for fast-food workers in 2024.

But during her latest interview, Snyder addressed the fears about In-N-Out, which maintains headquarters in California and Tennessee.

“There were rumors about ‘they’re gonna close all their California stores.’ I’m like what where did this even come from? That’s unimaginable. I can’t even imagine that — dumbest business decision ever,” she said.

Snyder added that In-N-Out continues to grow in California, with “lots of stores” slotted for the other cities in the state.

At the same time, the company has expanded to Nevada, Arizona, Utah, Texas, Oregon, Colorado, Idaho, Washington and Tennessee. Snyder suggested that Mississippi, Arkansas, and Oklahoma are under consideration, with New Mexico also in the works.

But she insisted the company is taking a slow and steady approach to growth that won’t compromise on the quality of its food her grandparents’ values, adding that In-N-Out won’t be able to accommodate every request to open a new location.

As for her own family’s relocation to Tennessee, Snyder described it as “kind of a God thing” and said she originally wanted to move to Colorado because she loves the mountains.

But her husband floated the idea of going to Tennessee instead. While they already had made plans, she recalled that “something just kind of clicked.”

“I felt it and then started looking at it, just praying, and I’m like ‘I think you’re right. I think that’s where we’re supposed to go,'” Snyder said.

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5489. Amazon plans its first large-scale data centers in Washington state as residents raise concerns

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 4, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:36 am

Amazon is moving toward building its first large-scale data centers in Washington state, with a proposed campus in Walla Walla County and a second in the Tri-Cities that the company confirmed this week.

The expansion into Amazon’s home state comes amid nationwide pushback against the rapid deployment of new AI data centers. Tuesday’s election underscored the scrutiny facing data center developers, with voters in communities across several states backing limits on new projects. In Eastern Washington, the Amazon proposals have drawn calls for greater environmental oversight and a temporary halt to data center development.

Amazon already has a substantial footprint in neighboring Oregon, where industry tracker Baxtel lists 64 AWS data center sites. Expansion there has divided communities, with residents pushing for restrictions over power and water concerns while some Eastern Oregon officials warn that slowing development would jeopardize jobs and tax revenue.

Both proposed Washington campuses would initially include three data center buildings. The Walla Walla County site covers roughly 134 acres in Wallula Gap, while the Tri-Cities campus is on a 1,000 acre property in the city of West Richland and could eventually grow to 21 buildings. The company is already operating smaller data centers in the state, including Seattle.

The Tri-City Herald first reported Monday that Amazon was behind the West Richland project. The company plans to hold a community open house Nov. 19 to discuss the proposal.

A full build-out of the West Richland campus could create more than 1,000 full-time data center jobs, Amazon said. Dallas real estate firm Trammell Crow initially purchased the property from the estate of agricultural businessman Frank Tiegs, who died in 2024, before selling it to Amazon.

Nearby residents have raised concerns about the planned campus, in part because of its proximity to about 200 homes. Residents asked the local city council to approve a temporary moratorium, but at a meeting Tuesday evening, council members adopted rules that removed a data center noise exemption, banned them in light industrial zones, and prohibited cryptocurrency mining. The council failed to pass a moratorium, NonStop Local reported.

Amazon says the upcoming open house will give residents an opportunity to ask questions about the planned development. A spokesperson described a “science fair” format, with booths hosted by experts discussing water and energy usage, job creation, noise and environmental impacts.

“We’re committed to growing responsibly and we want the community to leave the Open House with a better understanding of this project and what it could mean for the area,” the spokesperson said via email.

At Wallula Gap, a recent public-comment period offers an indication of the scrutiny Amazon faces.

Of the 706 submissions received during a 30-day comment period that closed Oct. 12, only 23 — about 3% — supported the project, according to an analysis by the Walla Walla Union-Bulletin. Most of the supportive comments came from the area, and many predicated their support on more stringent oversight of the proposed facility near the Columbia River.

More than 500 submissions came from outside Walla Walla County, according to the Union-Bulletin. Many included template language calling for an Environmental Impact Statement — a higher level of environmental assessment than currently required for the campus.

The proposed facility is located at the Wallula Gap Business Park, on property formerly owned by the Port of Walla Walla. The three proposed single-story data center buildings would create approximately 120 to 150 full-time jobs, Amazon said.

The land is zoned for “industrial agriculture – mixed” applications, which the company said includes data centers. Amazon’s involvement in the project was first reported by the Tri-City Herald in February.

Amazon’s FAQs for the two sites address several issues raised by residents, including electricity costs and water use.

Rising electric bills nationwide and the climate impacts of new gas power plants and backup diesel generators have made energy use a top concern. Amazon said it will work with local utilities and other officials “to ensure that our data centers do not raise electricity bills for people in our communities.”

The company reports that it matched all electricity consumed across its global operations with renewable energy sources in 2023 and 2024. That annual, company-wide accounting measure does not mean each facility runs on renewable electricity around the clock.

Amazon also points to its investment of “billions of dollars in nuclear energy projects,” including a proposed small modular reactor plant near the Tri-Cities that could come online in the 2030s.

“This project will provide net-new carbon-free energy for communities in the Pacific Northwest, including Eastern Washington,” Amazon said in its FAQ.

Amid concerns about water shortages, Amazon touts water-use rates that it says beat other tech companies and are much lower than irrigated farming. Those rates, however, do not include water used in electricity generation. Many power plants use water to produce steam that drives electricity-generating turbines and for cooling, with some water lost through evaporation.

At both locations, Amazon says it will pay 100% of its property taxes rather than seek tax breaks for building in the communities. The company says its taxes are higher than most industrial uses and directly support schools, roads, fire and police, and other services.

Beyond addressing concerns about its data centers, Amazon is making a broader case for why communities should welcome them. Last month, the company launched its Built Together initiative, committing more than $1 billion in additional investments over five years to U.S. communities where it operates data centers. The funding supports efforts including free community college, energy upgrades for homes and buildings, and workforce training.

In announcing the program, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman framed data center development as part of a global race for AI dominance. He warned that local and state moratoriums could harm the U.S. economy and national security.

“If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations,” Garman said. “As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”

In West Richland, residents will have an opportunity to question Amazon’s plans — and the assurances accompanying them — at the company’s upcoming open house.

Editor’s note: Story updated 11/5 to note that Amazon is operating smaller-scale data centers in Washington, but not campuses of the scope being proposed in Eastern Washington.

#5488. 15 state tax measures on 2026 ballots could reshape property and income bills

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A wealth tax, property tax caps, and income tax changes appear among 15 of the 33 tax measures on state ballots this fall.

Most years, the tax bill that lands in your mailbox reflects decisions lawmakers made far from your kitchen table. This November, some of those decisions shift onto the ballot itself. Voters in a long list of states will write the rules on their own, settling how much homeowners owe, how high income tax rates can climb, and who covers the bill for local government. A yes or no on a single line can reshape a household budget for years. A constitutional amendment can lock the outcome in place long after the campaign signs come down. Anyone who owns a home, earns a paycheck, runs a farm, or rents from someone who does has a stake in what happens.

Property taxes sit at the center of many of these contests. Many exemptions, freezes, and caps would transfer part of the load from one group of taxpayers to another. A break for one category of landholders can leave everyone else carrying a larger slice of what localities collect. A ceiling on assessment growth can limit what governments take in as market values rise. The proposals differ in scale. Some would nudge an eligibility threshold or tweak a technical formula. Others would rewrite how an entire state funds itself. Those who want to know where the burden falls need to look past the headline promise to the mechanics underneath.

Tax Foundation counts 33 tax-related measures on state ballots this fall and features 15 of them in a results table on its tracker. The group's experts plan to follow live returns for the most notable contests as votes come in. Some of the tracker's summaries walk through how a change would work in detail. Others list a measure by name alone. The 15 measures below form a selection drawn from the ones the tracker discusses. The list overlaps with the featured 15 without matching it, and it covers fewer than half of the full 33. Together these picks span wealth, income, and property taxes across nine states, from the West Coast to the Southeast. Each shows how one ballot choice could alter what residents pay.

Proposition 40 asks California voters to impose a one-time 5% levy on billionaires' wealth, a move that would give the U.S. its first wealth tax. Only residents worth $1 billion or more would face it. Every other Californian, including households with large but smaller fortunes, would sit outside its reach.

Residency on Jan. 1, 2026, determines who owes, and the value of each fortune on Dec. 31, 2026, sets the size of the bill. Moving away does not cancel the obligation. A billionaire who counted as a California resident on New Year's Day would owe after settling in another state months later. The residency snapshot predates the November vote. No one could dodge the measure by relocating after seeing it on the ballot.

Choosing the year's last day as the measuring point ties the amount owed to how each fortune fares across 2026. A gain during the year would enlarge the payment, and a loss would shrink it. Billionaires would not learn their final figure until the calendar closes, weeks after voters decide.

Tax Foundation warns that the design raises serious legal, administrative, and economic concerns. Its objections span the measure's whole life, from whether it survives in court to how the state tallies and gathers it to what it does to the wider economy. No other state has run a wealth tax. California would build its enforcement machinery without a domestic model to copy.

The state stands to collect revenue in the tens of billions of dollars, spread over several years, according to an estimate by the Legislative Analyst's Office. The office projects that working out what each billionaire owes and bringing in the payments could cost the state tens of millions of dollars a year for multiple years. New wealth tax receipts would cover that expense. A one-off assessment would carry a collection tail lasting years. At those scales, the paperwork bill would consume a sliver of what the tax delivers.

California Proposition 41 would forbid the state from enforcing any new tax that exempts itself from the Gann Limit, California's ceiling on state spending. The measure entered the ballot as a rival to Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax, and it bundles several provisions that reach beyond that spending rule.

The Gann Limit clause reaches any future tax drafted to escape the cap, including levies no one has written yet. It would bind the Legislature and voter-led campaigns alike. Lawmakers or citizens could approve a tax designed to sit outside the cap, yet the state would lack the power to collect it. Anyone crafting new revenue would need to fit it inside the existing limit for it to carry any force.

Proposition 41 would also order regular state audits of new special taxes to judge whether the programs they fund deliver results. Taxes that originate in ballot initiatives would face an extra checkpoint, an audit before the election. The sequence moves scrutiny of a citizen-backed tax ahead of the moment Californians decide its fate.

Proposition 41 targets the wealth tax head-on through a vote-count clause. Passage with more votes than Proposition 40 would let Proposition 41 invalidate the billionaire tax. A simple majority would not save Proposition 40 on its own. Both measures could clear the bar, and the wealth tax would still die if Proposition 41 drew the larger tally.

The clause turns the wealth tax question into a race between two vote totals. Each voter who backs both measures adds one vote to each side and does nothing to widen Proposition 40's lead. A Californian who wants the billionaire tax to survive gains the most by voting yes on it and no on Proposition 41. Opponents of the wealth tax face the mirror-image choice, yes on Proposition 41 and no on Proposition 40. Ballots that skip one of the two questions could tip a close contest.

California Proposition 43 would require two-thirds of voters to approve any local special tax that citizens place on the ballot. Today a simple majority decides those measures.

The higher threshold reaches every citizen-initiated local measure that creates a special tax, extends an existing one, or raises one. A campaign to renew a levy would need the same two-thirds margin as a campaign to start a new one. A special tax that voters approved under the majority rule would face the steeper climb the next time its backers sought an extension. Proposition 43 would write the requirement into the state constitution as an amendment.

Local governments in California already need two-thirds of the vote for special taxes they propose, according to the California Budget Center. A general tax clears with a bare majority. Under current rules, citizens drafting a special tax face a lower bar than local officials crafting the same kind of levy. Proposition 43 would erase that difference and hold both paths to a single standard.

The supermajority rule reshapes the math of a local campaign. A simple majority asks organizers to outpoll the opposition by a single vote. Under a two-thirds rule, opponents can sink a measure by holding anything above one-third of the ballots cast. Supporters would need two yes votes for every no vote to prevail. A special tax that wins a clear majority yet falls short of two-thirds would fail.

The measure, as described, targets special taxes alone. Nothing in its summary touches the simple-majority path for general taxes. Approval would leave every local special tax facing one supermajority hurdle, whoever writes it, and would widen the gap between what it takes to pass a special levy and a general one at the ballot box.

## Florida Amendment 3 offers the largest homestead break

Florida Amendment 3 would exempt up to $250,000 of a homestead's value from most property taxes, the largest homestead exemption anywhere in the U.S. The break would begin at $150,000 in 2027 and rise to $250,000 in 2028. Owners would wait a year at the lower level before reaching the larger figure.

School district levies sit outside the exemption. Homeowners would keep paying school taxes on their home's full value, while cities, counties, and other local taxing bodies would lose the exempted slice of their base. Schools would keep their funding base whole, and other local services would absorb the cut.

Jacksonville Mayor Donna Deegan expects the amendment to erase one-third of her city's budget, a $300 million hit, according to CNBC. She warns of deteriorating roads, closed libraries, pools, and parks, slower public safety response times, worse housing affordability, and more homelessness. Estimates put the statewide revenue loss at around $46 billion by 2032, according to CNBC. Hallandale Beach Mayor Joy Cooper asked residents on Nextdoor which city services they wanted to cut, and most replies urged officials to accept lower salaries.

Support for Amendment 3 erodes once voters hear what it could cost local government. A University of North Florida Public Opinion Research Lab poll found 61% in favor and 32% opposed when respondents heard it would phase out non-school homestead taxes, according to CNBC. After learning of projected city and county budget shortfalls across the state, respondents shifted to 45% support and 47% opposition. The 16-point drop in support turned a lopsided lead into a narrow deficit.

Gov. Ron DeSantis considers the amendment too modest. He first proposed a far bolder rollback that in time would have wiped out all property taxes on primary homes, with no carve-out for schools. Florida voters also face a second property tax amendment this fall. Amendment 3 sits between a governor who wanted deeper cuts and mayors bracing for lost services, and the poll's swing suggests the budget argument could decide the outcome.

Georgia Amendment 1 would let a single landowner classify up to 4,000 acres as bona fide conservation use property, double the 2,000-acre ceiling in effect today. Farming, timber production, and conservation all qualify as eligible uses. Owners at the current ceiling would gain room for up to 2,000 more acres under the preferential rules.

Enrolled tracts carry a lighter assessment through Georgia's Conservation Use Valuation Assessment program, known as CUVA, which sets their value at 40% of current use value. The appraisal turns on what the land does at present, whether it grows crops, raises timber, or sits in conservation. Georgia intends the favorable treatment to keep owners from converting agricultural land into homes or commercial sites under the weight of property tax bills. A higher cap would stretch that safeguard across more ground held by a single owner.

Owners who enroll in Rockdale County must swear a formal promise to keep the land in its present use. The county attaches the same pledge to residential transitional land. Each acre added under the new cap would come with the same sworn obligation in that county.

Owners with more than 2,000 qualifying acres stand to benefit from the higher cap. An owner with 4,000 qualifying acres can enroll no more than half of them under current law, leaving the other 2,000 outside CUVA's valuation. Passage would bring all 4,000 acres into the program. Owners with 2,000 qualifying acres or fewer fit under the existing limit and would see no change in how many acres they can enroll. Holdings beyond 4,000 acres would leave some land outside the program even after passage. The amendment trims the excluded portion for the largest owners without erasing it.

Louisiana voters will decide whether homeowners earning as much as $150,000 can lock in the assessed value of their homes, up from a $100,000 ceiling today. The change would lift the income limit by 50%.

Today's program confines its assessment freeze to owners whose incomes total $100,000 or less. A household a few dollars above that mark gets no freeze at all. Two neighbors with matching homes can face different assessment paths over a small gap in pay. The rule draws a hard line, and the amendment would move it without erasing it. Households crossing $150,000 would meet the same cliff that households crossing $100,000 meet now.

A higher cutoff would admit households earning more than $100,000 and up to $150,000, a $50,000 band the program now shuts out. No current participant would lose access. Every income under the old limit also clears the new one. Owners in the new band who qualify would see their home assessments hold steady from year to year.

The break gains worth the longer an owner keeps it in a rising market. A frozen assessment stays put while comparable homes climb in value. Each year prices rise, the distance between the frozen figure and the market widens. The freeze fixes one input to the tax bill and leaves the rate free to move. Owners inside the program can see bills change when local millage rates shift.

The new threshold would not take effect until tax year 2028. Until then, the existing limit keeps deciding who can claim the break. Newly eligible owners would wait outside the program through tax year 2027, even if voters approve the change in November.

Louisiana voters face five amendments on this fall's ballot. Among the three Louisiana measures in this list, this one alone makes household income the test for a property tax break.

A Louisiana amendment would set each locality's maximum millage rate for the coming year from the previous year's maximum allowed rate, beginning in tax year 2027. Under current law, the cap tracks the rate a local government levied the year before, even when officials charged less than the law allowed.

Today's formula penalizes restraint. A local government that charges below its limit in one year inherits a lower ceiling the next, and the shortfall follows it into later years. One lighter year can shrink the room officials have to raise revenue afterward, whatever their reasons for holding back.

The amendment would sever the link between what a locality collects and what it may collect later. Localities could keep millage under the cap in a given year and still carry the full maximum forward. Their taxing capacity would survive a low-rate year intact.

Taxpayers face both sides of the trade. Under current law, a year of reduced millage drags the following year's limit down with it. Under the amendment, the maximum would hold at its prior-year level. A cut in one year would no longer guarantee a lower ceiling in the next.

The measure governs ceilings alone. A yes vote would not by itself raise anyone's bill. Nothing in it sets the rate a locality charges. Local officials would keep deciding each year how much of their allowed capacity to use. What shifts is the starting point for that decision.

The current rule gives any locality that wants to preserve its future room a reason to levy the full amount each year. The amendment would remove that incentive. Under today's rules, each lean year resets the base, and a long string of them could leave a locality's ceiling below where it started. Voters would swap an automatic downward ratchet for more freedom to offer temporary relief without forfeiting later revenue.

## Louisiana lets veterans' spouses move an exemption once

Surviving spouses of disabled veterans in Louisiana would gain a one-time right to carry the disabled veteran homestead exemption to a different home, with the transferred break capped at its previous value. The amendment would let the benefit follow the spouse after a move. Without the amendment, a spouse who sells the family home has no path to bring the break along.

The cap governs how much moves with the spouse. A widow or widower who buys a pricier home would bring an exemption no larger than the one the household held before. Any value above that amount would remain taxable. A costlier purchase enlarges the taxable portion of the bill, not the break.

The single-transfer rule draws a second boundary. A spouse who uses the transfer and later relocates again would lose the right to take the exemption to a third property. One move marks the full extent of the new flexibility. A spouse weighing a downsize now and a later move closer to family would need to choose which relocation carries the break.

Neither limit widens eligibility. The proposal adds no new class of veterans or spouses and raises no dollar amount. It changes only where an existing benefit can sit. Local taxing bodies would exempt no more than they did before the move. The value shifts from one property's assessment to another's. Under the cap, the burden shift this measure creates stays narrow next to the property tax rewrites elsewhere on the ballot.

Louisiana voters will see this proposal among five amendments on the state's ballot. Its two limits let a surviving spouse hold on to the break after a move while capping the cost to the tax base at what the state had granted the household.

North Carolina voters will weigh a constitutional amendment ordering the General Assembly to pass a cap on the total property tax levy that local governments can impose. The legislature itself referred the question to voters. The amendment names no dollar figure. Future legislation would set the cap's terms, and lawmakers could carve out exceptions.

Every layer of local government that collects property tax falls within the requirement's reach. Counties, cities, and towns would face the eventual cap, as would special districts and any other local unit with authority to levy the tax. No type of local taxing body would escape it.

An existing North Carolina statute holds local property tax rates to $1.50 per $100 of assessed value. A rate ceiling governs the price charged on each dollar of value. It leaves total bills free to climb as assessments rise. The same rate applied to a larger base produces more revenue. A levy limit targets the total dollars collected. The amendment would add that second guardrail and keep the first in place.

Rising assessments expose the gap between the two tools. Under a rate ceiling alone, a locality whose property values grow can collect more money without touching its rate. A locality taxing below $1.50 can lift its rate and stay within the law. Depending on its design, a levy cap could restrain both routes to higher collections. It counts the dollars raised, whatever produced them.

The two restraints would rest on different legal footing. The duty to enact a levy cap would live in the constitution, while the rate ceiling stays in statute. Later sessions of the General Assembly would control the cap's details, yet the constitution would bind them to adopt one.

Tax Foundation points readers to material on how a well-designed levy limit could benefit taxpayers. The qualifier "well-designed" carries the weight in that framing. Any relief for property owners would hinge on the bill the General Assembly writes if voters approve the measure.

North Carolina voters will decide whether to cut the ceiling on the state's income tax rate from 7% to 3.5%. A rate cap sets the highest rate the state may charge, so the amendment targets the outer boundary lawmakers work within.

The proposed limit sits 3.5 percentage points below the current one. Any future push to raise the income tax rate past 3.5% would run into a cap half as high as today's.

The amendment shares the ballot with a second North Carolina proposal aimed at local property tax levies. Approval of both would place new constitutional restraints on the state income tax and on what local governments collect from property owners, all in a single election.

Oklahoma State Question 847 would cut the constitutional ceiling on yearly growth in the fair cash value of most locally assessed real property from 5% to 4%. Oklahoma bases each owner's property tax liability on fair cash value. The ceiling governs the pace at which the foundation of each bill can rise. Lawmakers referred the measure to voters as a constitutional amendment, and it would shave 1 percentage point off the current limit.

Homes that qualify for a homestead exemption and land classified as agricultural would absorb a steeper reduction. Their annual limit would drop from 3% to 1.75%, a decline of 1.25 percentage points. Against the current allowance, permitted yearly growth for those properties would shrink by nearly 42%. Most other real property would face a 20% trim.

The amendment would enlarge the gap between the two tracks. Today the general limit sits 2 percentage points above the one for homesteads and farmland. Under State Question 847, the spread would grow to 2.25 points. The preferred ceiling would fall to less than half the general one, 1.75% against 4%, compared with three-fifths under current law.

Modest percentage changes compound into wider differences over time. A property whose value rose by the maximum allowed amount five years in a row could gain about 27.6% under the current 5% limit. The proposed 4% ceiling would hold the same five-year climb to about 21.7%. The five-year maximum for homesteads and agricultural land would fall from about 15.9% to about 9.1%.

A 10-year horizon widens the divide. Most real property could gain no more than about 62.9% over 10 years under today's limit and about 48% under the new one. Homesteads and farmland would slide from about 34.4% to about 18.9% over the same stretch. On either horizon, owners of homesteads and farmland would give up more than 40% of their potential growth in taxable value, about twice the share other owners would lose.

Oklahoma homeowners over 65 who pass an income test receive a full freeze on the fair cash value of their homestead, and State Question 847 would swap that test for a tiered scale tied to household income. The constitution draws a single line today. Seniors on the qualifying side see no yearly growth in the value that sets their property tax bill. Those on the other side get nothing from the senior provision, no matter how close their earnings sit to the cutoff.

Lower-income seniors would keep the complete freeze under the amendment. Their homestead values would stay fixed from one year to the next, as they do today. The measure leaves the bottom of the income scale alone and directs its change at households the existing test excludes. Stripping out the old eligibility requirements means no senior over 65 would stand outside the protection.

Higher-income seniors would gain a ceiling on valuation growth where they have no senior protection today. State Question 847 would hold their annual increases to between 0.35% and 1.75%, with household income setting each homeowner's exact limit. The top of that band is five times the bottom. A household's tier would decide whether its home value inches up by a fraction of a percent or climbs to match the cap the measure sets for other homesteads.

Household earnings would determine how much relief each senior gets, a shift from today's on-off switch. Seniors above the old cutoff would pick up a safeguard they lack now, and seniors below it would give up nothing. Lawmakers placed the change before voters as a legislatively referred constitutional amendment. Its tiers would live in the constitution itself. The overhaul turns Oklahoma's senior break from a benefit some households receive and others miss into one that tapers as household income rises.

Wyoming Initiative 1 would layer a 50% exemption on the value of an owner-occupied house on top of the homestead break lawmakers adopted in 2025. The add-on carries no value cap and applies to the structure alone. The land beneath the home gets none of the added benefit.

The 2025 law sets the baseline. It exempts 25% of the first $1 million in fair market value for owner-occupied single-family residences, a break that tops out at $250,000. Owners must live in the home at least eight months a year to qualify. Initiative 1 lowers that occupancy threshold to six months for its own exemption. The two-month cut would extend the new break to owners who live in their homes six or seven months a year, a group the 2025 law leaves out.

Eligible homeowners could claim both breaks at once. The first trims taxable value by a quarter of the property's entire worth, up to the $1 million mark. The second strips out half the house's value with no ceiling. Owners of homes valued above $1 million gain nothing extra from the 2025 exemption, yet the uncapped 50% break keeps growing with the value of the house. Properties where the building, not the acreage, makes up most of the worth would capture the largest share of the relief.

Wyoming's residential property taxes sit among the lowest in the country, according to Tax Foundation. Initiative 1 would trim bills that start near the bottom of the national scale.

Wyoming policymakers have worried for years that the state depends too much on unstable revenue from oil, gas, and mining. Tax Foundation argues that Initiative 1 would deepen that overreliance. Shrinking the residential tax base would leave a larger share of the state's income resting on those volatile sources. A slump in oil, gas, or mining would hit a budget left with less homeowner revenue to cushion it.

Colorado voters will decide this fall whether to drop the state's flat income tax. The question reaches the basic architecture of how Colorado taxes earnings, a deeper change than the assessment caps, exemptions, and vote thresholds that fill most of this list.

Colorado shares the income tax spotlight in this selection with North Carolina. North Carolina's amendment addresses how high the state's rate may climb. Colorado's measure asks whether a single flat rate should survive at all, which makes it the only question here aimed at the structure of an income tax itself.

Washington state voters will decide whether to keep a newly adopted 9.9% tax on millionaires. The question asks the electorate to judge a levy that already exists. Keeping it would leave the 9.9% rate in force. Rejecting it would undo a policy the state only recently put in place.

Millionaires would carry the levy's burden, while the choice to keep it rests with every voter. Its newness also sets this contest apart. California voters will settle whether to create a wealth tax from scratch. Washington voters will judge one the state has already adopted.

Massachusetts voters confront a related question about their own millionaire's surtax. Their ballot asks whether its revenue counts under the Commonwealth's revenue limit, a question that assumes the surtax stays. Washington's ballot goes further and asks whether its tax continues at all. Of the two states putting millionaire levies before voters, only Washington lets the electorate end one outright.

#5487. Alabama Power spent more than $6 million on ads last year — and customers can be billed for half of them until 2029

This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.

On a busy election day, the Alabama Public Service Commission requested that Alabama Power voluntarily stop billing customers, effective immediately, for television commercials and other ads it buys to promote various aspects of its business.

Alabama Power is the largest electricity provider in Alabama, with territory covering about two-thirds of the state. Though it is a monopoly, the company spends millions each year on advertising, touting its reliability, customer service and other aspects of its business.

In recent months, the company has launched a series of television commercials touting a rate freeze it announced late last year amid heavy criticism over rising electricity prices.

A state law passed earlier this year will prohibit Alabama Power from including the costs of those commercials in customers’ electric bills, meaning the powerful utility will have to find all of the dollars in corporate profits. But the new law won’t take effect until 2029.

Currently, Alabama Power is allowed to bill customers for half of its non-public safety advertising costs.

During Tuesday’s meeting, PSC President Cynthia Lee Almond moved to “request” that Alabama Power voluntarily begin excluding those costs immediately.

“I don’t see any reason why we shouldn’t go ahead and take steps now to begin that process, rather than waiting until Jan. 1, 2029,” Almond said during the meeting.

Almond then made her motion, which was not on the meeting agenda, but came after the regular report from the commission’s electricity division.

“I move that the commission request that Alabama Power consent to exclude all advertising expenses from retail rate setting until after Dec. 31, 2028, when the new law takes effect,” Almond said. “Assuming Alabama Power consents, this interim measure would be reflected in its [Rate Stabilization and Equalization] filings for 2027 and 2028.”

Commissioners Jeremy Oden and Chris Beeker IV voted yes after a brief discussion.

According to the company filings with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Alabama Power spent more than $6 million in general advertising last year, roughly $4 per customer. It’s unclear from the federal filing how much of that total was passed on to customers or how much might be impacted by the new prohibition.

Alabama Power did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Daniel Tait, executive director of Energy Alabama, said the move was a boon to Alabama Power customers, who faced some of the highest electric bills in the country in recent years.

“We are grateful for the leadership of President Almond and the full commission for acting to end customers paying for Alabama Power’s advertising,” Tait said. “Once in place, Alabama will have one of the strongest customer protections in the nation on this front.”

This will be among the last actions of the commission under its current construction before a major overhaul takes effect.

In January, the commission will expand from three members to seven. Outgoing Gov. Kay Ivey has appointed four new commissioners, who will take office in January, including the PSC’s two first-ever Black members.

Oden and Beeker will also leave the commission in January after being defeated in Republican primaries. Cullman County Sheriff Matt Gentry will take Oden’s Place 1 seat, and former state auditor and PSC Commissioner Jim Zeigler will replace Beeker in Place 2.

Zeigler, a perennial candidate in Alabama across several decades, will return to the commission 48 years after leaving the PSC. He served one term from 1975-1979, during an era of skyrocketing energy costs and protracted political battles over electric rates between Alabama Power and then-Gov. George Wallace.

Almond will be the sole remaining member of the current commission.

The new seven-member commission will be overseen by the state’s first secretary of energy, who will be selected by Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville. The new secretary will set the commission agenda, and overruling the secretary will require a vote of five of seven commissioners.

Tuberville has not yet announced his pick for secretary of energy. The only statutory requirement is that the secretary “must have experience in utility regulation or energy policy or a related field.”
