#5486. Ai2 gets $5M from Google to turn AI weather model into a tool for projecting climate change

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 5, 2026 at 2:27 pm

Google is giving Seattle’s Allen Institute for AI about $5 million in funding, plus another $1.8 million in cloud credits, to turn an AI weather model developed by Google Research into a tool for projecting climate change decades into the future.

The money will help Ai2 build an open-source model designed to give scientists, water agencies and other planners a faster, more accurate look at how rainfall, temperatures and water supplies could change over the next five to 50 years.

Announced Wednesday morning, the three-year project pairs funding from Google.org, the company’s philanthropic arm, with technical support from Google Research. Ai2 will add four people to its eight-person climate modeling team to do the work.

Google’s work on the model centers on weather, looking ahead a year at most. It has less interest and expertise in climate projections that run decades into the future, said Oliver Watt-Meyer, Ai2’s director of research for AI climate modeling.

“Climate modeling is a bit more of a public good,” he said. “It is information that people need to know, but it’s often more government agencies that are thinking about this.”

Starting with Google’s model: Ai2’s model, NeuralGCM+, will build on Google’s NeuralGCM, which mixes traditional physics equations with AI. Watt-Meyer, who wrote about NeuralGCM for the journal Nature when Google published its research in 2024, said the model does well at forecasting weather and at recreating past climate.

In that piece, he also pointed out its limits: some of its long runs broke down, and when researchers simulated ocean temperatures about 7 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than today, its predictions for the atmosphere didn’t make physical sense.

Under the new project, Ai2 will try to fix both problems. It will connect NeuralGCM+ to an ocean and sea ice model, with the goal of running stable simulations that span decades. It will also build more established physics into the model, then check its predictions for a warmer world against results from traditional climate models.

Ai2’s climate team is made up largely of atmospheric scientists, with the engineers and computing power of an AI institute behind them.

Ai2 is “uniquely positioned to extend Google’s NeuralGCM model into the next generation of long-term climate projections,” said Alex Diaz, head of applied science at Google.org, in a statement, citing the institute’s climate science expertise and commitment to open research.

Where the idea started: The team’s origins go back to the late Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen, who took an interest in climate modeling before his death in 2018. His company, then known as Vulcan, launched the climate modeling project in 2019, and the group moved to Ai2 in 2021. Allen had founded the nonprofit AI institute in 2014.

The original plan was to combine physics and AI. The group set that aside because the AI couldn’t be trained well inside older climate models written in Fortran, a decades-old programming language. Google wrote NeuralGCM in modern code that solves that problem.

In that way, Watt-Meyer said, “This is actually kind of coming full circle for us.”

Ai2 already has its own family of AI climate models, called the Ai2 Climate Emulator, or ACE. These models rely entirely on AI and run much faster than NeuralGCM. But versions trained only on historical data struggle to project a climate the planet hasn’t experienced yet.

Watt-Meyer said NeuralGCM’s design could hold up better as the world warms, because the laws of physics built into it won’t change.

The timeline: The first step is releasing the code for training NeuralGCM, which has been tied to Google’s internal systems. Making it public will let other researchers train their own versions, including on common GPUs rather than only Google’s own chips. Ai2 expects to release it within the first year, with work on the ocean model running in parallel.

Making the model reliable in a warmer world is the hardest part, and it could take longer than three years. “We don’t know if it’ll work necessarily,” Watt-Meyer said.

He said AI coding agents are changing what his team thinks it can get done in that time. The tools are well suited to translating old code into modern programming languages. In one case, an outside group converted a well-known ocean model from Fortran into the same language NeuralGCM uses, so Ai2 won’t have to build its own.

Watt-Meyer called the tools “a real game changer” for simulation. “It’s kind of a golden era for this kind of scientific computing,” he said.

Google Research will keep developing NeuralGCM for forecasts of a few weeks to a year, and the two teams will share training code and data. One of Google’s lead NeuralGCM researchers is spending three days at Ai2 this week.

Who would use the model: Watt-Meyer pointed to questions such as how rainfall could change in the Southwest, a key issue for water planning around Lake Powell on the Colorado River. Insurance and reinsurance companies already use Ai2’s ACE models in their research.

Asked whether data center developers could use these kinds of models, Watt-Meyer said they could help answer questions about cooling, access to renewable energy and risks such as extreme weather and rising seas. But it isn’t clear if the industry is paying attention.

“There’s so much frantic energy to build these things as fast as possible,” he said. “I’m not sure people are really seriously considering this kind of climate data, though maybe they should be a bit more.”

Correction: An earlier version of this story gave an incorrect date for the start of the climate modeling effort at Vulcan. It started in 2019.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5485. So much ‘liquid gold’ could hit the market that the world’s top producer is withholding output—but supplies can’t stay ‘extra virgin’ for long

A bumper harvest of olives threatens to jolt the olive oil market, prompting the world’s top producer to suppress supplies for the first time ever.

On Friday, Spain’s agriculture ministry ordered farmers to hold back 12% of their production until the end of September 2027, requiring them to store supplies on their farms or at third-party facilities.

“The measure aims to ensure farmers’ profitability and also to protect the interests of olive oil buyers,” it said, according to the Financial Times, adding that “greater stability to the market” will benefit producers and consumers.

While the move is unprecedented, the European Union allows olive oil supplies to be held back, unless it leads to excessive market distortion.

The current harvest season for so-called “liquid gold” began in September, and favorable weather this past spring promises to reverse years of drought and heat that kept olive production low.

This season, Spanish olive oil production is projected to jump 23% to 1.6 millions tons, marking the fourth-largest harvest ever. The agriculture ministry seeks to keep 188,000 tons off the market.

But expectations for more supply have already sent olive oil prices down. At mills in Andalusia, they averaged 2.93 euros per kilogram last weekend, down about 15% in about two months.

The olive oil industry has pushed back against the government’s attempt to prop up prices, pointing out the market is global while the order only applies to Spanish producers.

Kyle Holland, senior analyst at commodity data firm Expana, also noted that olive oil degrades over time, telling that FT that after several months in storage ”very quickly that olive oil is not going to be extra virgin anymore.”

He added that top olive oil buyers already have hefty supplies, so ordering farmers to store away some production would have little immediate impact on prices.

Spain isn’t the only country dealing with wild swings in key commodities.

The Quebec Maple Syrup Producers, which oversees Canada’s strategic syrup reserve, recently warned the stockpile will be completely empty by February.

While new supplies will continue to be produced, the reserve won’t be able to help ease any wobbles in output, which depends heavily on the weather and can be volatile.

Demand has increased in recent years as producers have diversified to more market beyond the U.S., but last year saw an especially big spike after President Donald Trump launched his global trade war.

To get ahead of anticipated tariffs, Americans rushed to buy up Canadian syrup supplies. As a result, total syrup exports jumped nearly 16% last year, up from 9% growth in 2024.

Meanwhile, the Iran war has forced oil-consuming countries around the world to drain crude stockpiles. In the U.S., the Strategic Petroleum Reserve has fallen to the lowest level since 1982.

Elsewhere, Japan has a rice reserve that had to be drawn down last year as prices soared amid bad weather and looming threats from natural disasters that sparked panic buying. But this year, Japan has already swung to a record surplus.

And China tapped its strategic pork reserve in 2019 after an outbreak of swine fever sent prices higher. But this year, prices have slumped as the anemic consumer economy has weighed on demand while the government’s prior encouragement to boost production has now resulted in oversupply.

Pork prices have plunged 39% over the last four years. To help prop up the market, China has repeatedly purchased pork for the strategic reserve.

Jason Ma is the weekend editor at Fortune, where he covers markets, the economy, finance, and housing.

#5484. 5 awkward moments everyone has faced (and how to recover)

Free daily briefing on global business news.

rom forgetting names to sending an embarrassing email, learn how to handle uncomfortable moments with confidence, honesty, and grace

Everyone has an embarrassing moment they'd rather forget.

Maybe you blank on someone's name right after they've greeted you, send a message to the one person who definitely shouldn't see it or make an awkward social misstep in front of a crowd. However it happens, that sudden rush of embarrassment can make you wish the floor would open up and swallow you.

The good news is that most awkward moments feel much bigger to the person experiencing them than to everyone else. And while you can't always prevent a social slipup, you can control how you respond. A little honesty, a sincere apology or a well-timed decision not to make a scene can go a long way toward getting through the moment.

Reader’s Digest offers etiquette advice for some of life's most uncomfortable situations, with practical ways to take responsibility, avoid making things worse and move on with your dignity intact. The common thread? Don't panic, don't overexplain and don't turn one awkward moment into an even bigger production.

Here are five embarrassing situations you might recognize—and how to handle them with a little more grace.

Few things are more awkward than running into someone who greets you by name when you have absolutely no idea what to call them. Pretending you remember can make the conversation even more uncomfortable, especially if the person clearly knows you've met before.

Reader’s Digest recommends being straightforward rather than trying to bluff your way through the introduction. A simple, “I'm having one of those days—could you remind me of your name?” is often enough. If you remember where you met, mention it. That helps show you recognize the person even if their name has temporarily slipped your mind.

If you've just met someone and realize you've already forgotten their name, there are a couple of ways to avoid the same problem later. In a professional setting, suggest exchanging business cards. In a more casual situation, swap phone numbers and let the other person enter their information directly into your phone.

And if neither option feels natural, honesty is still better than pretending. Admit that you're having a momentary brain freeze and move on with the conversation. Most people understand that names can be difficult to remember, especially when you're meeting several people at once.

The trick is to address the situation quickly and casually. The longer you try to hide the fact that you've forgotten someone's name, the more attention you may end up drawing to it.

Few workplace mistakes inspire instant regret quite like sending a private email to the person it was about. Maybe you vented about your boss to a colleague and accidentally copied your boss instead. Or perhaps a message meant for a friend landed in a professional inbox. Either way, there's no unsending the awkwardness once the recipient has read it.

Reader’s Digest recommends owning the mistake as soon as you realize what happened. If the message went to your boss, contact them directly rather than hoping they'll ignore it. Explain the circumstances honestly, whether you were frustrated about a meeting or overwhelmed by extra work. Apologize and acknowledge that you should have addressed your concerns with them directly.

Trying to pretend the email meant something else or offering an elaborate excuse is unlikely to help. A straightforward explanation shows that you're willing to take responsibility for what you sent.

Of course, prevention is better than damage control. Reader’s Digest also recommends saving a message as a draft and rereading it before hitting send. Double-check the recipient line, especially when you're replying quickly or sending something sensitive.

And if you're angry or frustrated, resist the urge to vent in writing. Pick up the phone and talk to a trusted friend instead. Emails can be misdirected, forwarded or saved, so they're rarely the best place to let off steam.

You know about the birthday party, anniversary trip or baby shower, and somehow the secret comes out before the guest of honor is supposed to know. It's an uncomfortable feeling, especially when you realize you've spoiled something someone else worked hard to plan.

If there's a chance to recover the surprise, Reader’s Digest suggests trying to reintroduce a little uncertainty without inventing an elaborate lie. You might say you misunderstood what you heard or that the plans haven't actually been confirmed. The goal is to give the other person a reason not to assume the surprise is ruined.

But don't create a bigger deception to cover the original mistake. If the person already knows what's happening, accept responsibility and apologize. Depending on the situation, you may also need to contact the host and explain what happened so they can decide how to handle it.

There is one important consideration: The person planning the surprise may prefer to keep the situation quiet. If the honoree is willing to act surprised when the event arrives and asks you not to tell anyone else, respect that request.

You can't always put the secret back once it's out, but you can avoid making the situation worse. A sincere apology and a little discretion are usually better than a complicated cover story.

You tell a friend you can't make dinner, only to end up at happy hour with someone else. Then a photo appears on social media, and suddenly your explanation for skipping the original plans doesn't look quite so convincing.

If the friend confronts you, Reader’s Digest recommends telling the truth. Maybe you were exhausted and didn't have the energy for a long evening, but felt up to a spontaneous, shorter get-together later. Perhaps another commitment ended earlier than expected. Whatever the reason, explain it honestly and as kindly as you can.

If you simply weren't in the mood for the original plans, it's better to admit that than invent an excuse. You can also make it clear that you still value the friendship and suggest another time to get together.

Canceling one commitment specifically to make plans with someone else is harder to explain. Reader’s Digest notes that this is particularly rude, so if you find yourself in that situation, you'll need a genuinely good reason to ask to reschedule. Be upfront about what happened, ask rather than assume your friend will understand, and consider treating them when you finally meet up as a gesture of appreciation.

The bigger lesson is to be considerate when making and changing plans. People are more likely to understand an honest explanation than a story that falls apart as soon as they see a photo.

Few social moments feel quite as awkward as misreading a greeting. You lean in for a hug, only to realize the other person is reaching out for a handshake. Suddenly, you're both caught in an uncomfortable dance, unsure which gesture to commit to.

The best way to handle it? Don't make it a bigger deal than it is. A quick laugh and a friendly comment can smooth things over. You might say, “Looks like we had different plans there!” Then move on with the conversation rather than replaying the moment.

Reader’s Digest reminds readers that these small social missteps happen to everyone. Most people aren't judging you as harshly as you might imagine, and a little humor can help everyone feel more at ease.

#5483. First X-BAT fighter jet prototype unveiled as Shield AI preps Seattle area factory for 2027 launch

by John Cook on Nov 4, 2026 at 8:26 amNovember 4, 2026 at 8:41 am

Defense technology startup Shield AI has completed its first full-scale prototype of the X-BAT autonomous fighter jet as the company prepares its manufacturing and engineering hub south of Seattle.

Constructed in 12 months at a facility in Frisco, Texas, the prototype is currently en route to the company’s flight-test center at Newton City-County Airport in Kansas.

The milestone keeps Shield AI on track for its major manufacturing push in the Seattle area, one that it says could employ 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s.

In late September, the company announced a 420,000-square-foot facility dubbed “X-Forge 3” at the Des Moines Creek Business Park, which is scheduled to open in spring 2027. The company has already posted dozens of Seattle-area job openings across avionics, mechanical design, software engineering and aircraft manufacturing.

The unveiling of the X-BAT prototype keeps the company on schedule for its planned regional buildout in Des Moines, a spokesperson tells GeekWire.

“This milestone represents a year of sustained effort and discipline from a team that committed to an ambitious design and build schedule and delivered,” Armor Harris, senior vice president of aircraft engineering at Shield AI, said in a blog post. “That is no small feat.”

San Diego-based Shield AI expects the first X-BAT aircraft to roll off the line in Des Moines in 2028, with full production ramping up to about 150 aircraft per year by the early 2030s, Harris told GeekWire in an interview in September.

It’s an extremely ambitious timeline, but one the company says is necessary given the changing dynamics of warfare.

“The team is laser focused on keeping pace because we know a capability is only useful if it arrives in time to matter,” Harris said. “We cannot take decades to develop an aircraft when the need is already here. That urgency has shaped how we approach the engineering work, and how we work with partners in the U.S. government.”

Unveiled last year, the X-BAT is an AI-piloted strike fighter that takes off and lands vertically, carries up to 2,000-pound class weapons in internal bays, and is designed for a 1,000-nautical-mile combat radius — which, when it takes flight, would top the estimated 590 nautical mile combat radius of the Lockheed Martin F-35A.

One of its key tactical advantages is the ability to take off and land without concrete runways — hence the tagline for the X-BAT: “Earth is our Runway.”

The X-BAT launches from and returns to a mobile, trailer-mounted Launch and Recovery Vehicle, which allows the AI-piloted jet to deploy from cargo ships, naval destroyers or remote areas where it’s too costly or dangerous to build traditional runways.

“Our adversaries have invested in long range missiles that put our aircraft at risk when they’re on the ground. Aircraft are hard to shoot down in the air, but easy to destroy when they’re on the ground,” Harris notes in the blog post. “X-BAT is the answer to this threat because it forces the adversary to take all those assets that are overhead looking down at our airbases and makes them try to go and find where the X-BATs are hiding.”

Last month, the U.S. Navy awarded Shield AI a $150 million contract modification through the Pentagon’s Defense Exportability Features program, matched dollar-for-dollar by $150 million in private Shield AI funds. Alongside a prior $100 million joint Navy and Defense Innovation Unit award in August, total program backing stands at approximately $400 million.

Co-founded by former Navy SEAL Brandon Tseng, Shield AI raised a $2 billion venture capital round at a $12.7 billion valuation earlier this year.

With the prototype built, Shield AI’s engineering team is focusing on proving out its vertical-takeoff-and-landing mechanics in Kansas ahead of initial flight trials later this year.

Harris detailed a multi-phase testing campaign ahead:

“We’ve built the first aircraft,” Harris wrote. “Now it’s time to go prove what it can do.”

#5482. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5481. ‘No vote, no warning, just plain math’: Social Security is six years from an automatic 22% cut—and most Americans have no idea

More than one in five Americans don’t know that their Social Security checks could be cut by roughly 20% in about six years, according to a recent TIAA survey on Social Security.

The program’s retirement trust fund, which pays benefits to retirees and survivors, is projected to run out of reserves in the fourth quarter of 2032, according to the 2026 Social Security Trustees Report. After that, incoming payroll taxes would cover only 78% of scheduled benefits. The resulting 22% cut would apply across the board, including to people already collecting.

“Insolvency is a slightly misleading word for what the Trustees are projecting,” says Martin Mulyadi, YHB Endowed Chair in Accounting and Professor of Accounting at Shenandoah University. Payroll taxes keep flowing after 2032, he notes: “Social Security is not running out of money in 2032. It is running out of savings.”

The stakes are large. Social Security pays monthly benefits to more than 71 million people, and it provides the majority of income for 43% of seniors, according to AARP. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) estimates that a 22% cut would cost a typical dual-income couple retiring in 2033 about $16,900 a year.

CRFB has warned that the program is “on a collision course toward insolvency,” and Fortune has reported that its finances haven’t looked this bad since 1983. The alarm grew louder after the trustees confirmed the 22% cut in June.

“America has a 25 trillion dollar problem,” says Michael Liner, a disability attorney and founder of Liner Legal, a law firm that specializes in Social Security disability benefits. “The gap between what Social Security has promised and what it can actually afford to pay.”

The trustees now put that 75-year gap even higher, at $29.3 trillion in present value, up from $25.1 trillion in last year’s report. If nothing changes, Liner says, the cut arrives automatically: “No vote, no warning, just plain math.” For many retirees, he adds, it will be “the difference between getting by or not.”

Social Security is funded mainly by payroll taxes. For decades, those taxes exceeded what the program paid out, and the surplus built up reserves in two trust funds: the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance (OASI) fund for retirees and survivors, and the Disability Insurance (DI) fund.

That changed in 2021, when the retirement fund’s costs began exceeding its total income, according to the Congressional Research Service. Reserves have been covering the difference ever since.

“In 2025, Social Security took in about $1.45 trillion and paid out about $1.61 trillion, and reserves covered the gap,” Mulyadi says.

The disability fund is in better shape; the trustees don’t project it running dry at any point in the next 75 years. If Congress legally merged the two funds, combined reserves would last until 2034 and then cover 83% of benefits, according to CRFB. That would require a change in law, and it wouldn’t close the underlying shortfall.

The public has noticed. In a June 2025 survey, just 36% of Americans told AARP they were confident in Social Security’s future, the lowest level since 2010.

Much of the pressure is demographic. Social Security now serves roughly twice as many beneficiaries as it did in 1980, when about 35.5 million people collected. Lower birth rates mean fewer workers paying in, retirees are collecting for longer, and declining immigration has shrunk the pool of workers paying payroll taxes.

Inequality plays a role, too. Payroll taxes apply only to earnings up to a cap, $184,500 this year, and high earners’ pay has grown faster than everyone else’s. The share of total wages subject to the tax fell from almost 87% in 1984 to roughly 83% today, according to Roosevelt Institute research reported by CBS News.

“The Social Security trust fund is under strain because Congress has failed to update the program for the economy we actually have,” said Elizabeth Wilkins, CEO of the Roosevelt Institute, a progressive think tank. “Too much income now flows to the top, where it escapes Social Security taxation.”

The last time Social Security came this close, Congress acted. The 1983 amendments gradually raised the full retirement age from 65 to 67 and, for the first time, subjected some benefits to federal income tax.

“We’ve had two instances in our history where it was suggested Social Security was going to go insolvent,” says Ernie Wingard, an advisor at Capital Choice Financial Group, “and in both of those instances, at the last minute, Congress was able to come to an agreement that saved it.”

That 1983 fix was designed to keep the program solvent for 75 years. If the retirement fund runs dry in 2032 as projected, it will have lasted about 50.

Lawmakers have plenty of levers. Options modeled in the American Academy of Actuaries’ Social Security Challenge tool and in Social Security Administration analyses include:

“Any fix has to close that gap through some mix of more revenue, such as a higher payroll tax rate or a higher cap on taxable earnings, and slower benefit growth, such as a later full retirement age or changes to the benefit formula,” Mulyadi says. “Each option has trade-offs, and the longer Congress waits, the larger each adjustment has to be.”

The fight is over the mix. In a debate covered by Fortune, two economists who disagreed on whether to phase out Social Security still agreed that wealthy Americans would have to pay more. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, meanwhile, argued in June that economic growth can shore up the program without benefit cuts.

“This is absolutely something that can be fixed,” says Nancy LeaMond, AARP’s executive vice president and chief advocacy and engagement officer. “Congress has hundreds of tools in its toolbox to strengthen Social Security and fill that gap of 20 percent or so without cutting the payments that Americans have earned for a lifetime of hard work.”

“This should be a wake-up call: Congress needs to act,” AARP CEO Myechia Minter-Jordan said in a June statement. “Americans have worked hard and paid into Social Security their entire lives, and they deserve to count on it when they retire.”

Whatever lawmakers choose, they have about six years to choose it.

For households, Mulyadi recommends planning with a range rather than a single number. “Log in to your my Social Security account at ssa.gov, look at your projected benefit, and test your retirement budget at about 75 to 80% of it,” he says.

“If the plan still works, a cut is an inconvenience,” he says. “If it doesn’t, you still have time to save more, work a little longer, or rethink when to claim.”

#5480. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5479. Millennials want to quit corporate jobs for nonprofits. The problem is pay

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Millennials are increasingly disillusioned with corporate life and considering nonprofits for work. But the difference in pay is often prohibitive

Millennials have spent about 20 years building their careers, and for many of them, their pay has mostly plateaued. Glassdoor senior economist Chris Martin told Fortune in September that millennial pay has "for the most part peaked" and from here will grow only about as fast as inflation until they stop working. Millennials can now tell themselves "we've made it," he said, "and the long and the short of it is, it doesn't feel good." The disappointment has many of them reconsidering the work they're doing. When Glassdoor polled its community this summer, 76% of millennials said they're seriously rethinking the direction their careers have gone.

Many tech workers had no choice but to leave the corporate world this year. The decision was made for them. Andy Challenger, a workplace expert and chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas, an outplacement firm that tracks layoff announcements, has watched job cuts pile up all year. The pace of layoffs slowed almost everywhere else, but tech companies announced about one and a half times as many U.S. job cuts from January through September as they had over the same months of 2025, according to the firm's September report. "Tech remains the center of gravity for this year's cuts, Challenger said, "and AI is still the reason companies give."

The nonprofits that some of those workers might turn to for more meaningful work are laying off staff too. Nonprofits announced more job cuts in September than in any other month this year and about seven times as many as they had in September 2025. For a millennial who wants to trade a corporate job for one of a higher calling, the switch is harder to land and harder to afford. Millennials who want to leave the business world are mostly building backup careers on the side. The ones who can leave a full-time job tend to be the ones with family money or a spouse's paycheck to fall back on.

Millennials want their work to stand for something, and many have turned down an employer over it. In Deloitte Global's 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey of adults in 44 countries, taken from November 2025 to January 2026, 97% of millennials said finding purpose in their work matters to their well-being and to how satisfied they are with their jobs. Yet around 60% say their current job doesn't match what they believe. Another 40% say they turned down a potential employer, an assignment, or a project over their personal ethics, and that has held steady in every edition of the survey since 2023.

Many millennials can't afford to go without a paycheck while they look for work that means more to them. Nearly half of the Gen Z and millennial respondents in the same survey said they live paycheck to paycheck, and cost of living was their top worry for the fifth year in a row. "They feel really insecure in their jobs. Many are not in a position to be unemployed or strike out on their own," said Martin, the Glassdoor economist. A worker who can't miss a paycheck can't quit first and look for the next job later.

So the millennials who want change are mostly testing it while they keep the job they have. Glassdoor's latest Millennial Report calls the approach "stability stacking." Workers build up skills, income, contacts, and other job prospects at the same time, and if they lose one job, they still have the rest to fall back on. They learn AI skills, move sideways into a different role, or get known in the field they want to join, all while still drawing a paycheck. "Stability stacking is a response to this moment of, 'I thought it would feel better. I thought I could count on my career and feel stable,'" Martin added.

Kat Clark, a former Apple $AAPL senior manager who started a nonprofit for teachers in 2022, needed a side income and a cheaper state to make the switch work. Clark told Business Insider in 2023 that she joined Apple in 2019 owing more than $100,000 in business-school loans. She paid off all of it before she quit in July 2022, giving up what she called "a couple hundred-thousand dollars per year." The next month she launched Teachers in Their Power, which draws attention to the problems teachers face. Without the Apple salary, she could no longer afford to live in San Francisco, so she moved to Wisconsin and took on part-time work as a marketing executive for hire and as a consultant for education technology startups. "The biggest sacrifice I made was leaving the Bay Area," she said.

Nonprofit leaders say they get plenty of applicants but too few with the skills the job needs. In a fall 2025 survey by PNP Staffing Group and Careers In Nonprofits, leaders said they struggle to find people who know fund accounting — the bookkeeping nonprofits use to track restricted grants and donations — and those who offer bilingual services, work in affordable housing, or hold a clinical license. Some leaders also worry that people are using AI to make fake applications. Going through a big stack of them, those leaders have to sort out not just who's qualified but who's real.

Where a corporate worker's experience does fit — notably in finance roles — nonprofits say they can't pay what the market pays. Low pay was the most common reason hiring was hard in 2025, and it hurt most in fundraising jobs, finance jobs, and jobs that require a license, according to PNP Staffing Group. People are quitting fundraising, finance, and technology jobs at high rates, and nonprofits also take a long time to fill similar roles. At many of them, hiring runs past a month while leaders wait on shifting grant money and approvals. The firms said that's long enough for the best candidates to take other offers.

The nonprofit jobs that come close to corporate pay sit at the top of the biggest organizations, and the jobs below them pay a fraction of that. At the biggest nonprofits in Washington, D.C., those with budgets over $50 million, chief financial officers earned more than four times what bookkeepers did in fall 2025, according to PNP Staffing Group's salary tables. Staff accountants and database managers at nonprofits in New York and D.C. mostly earned well under six figures. Each nonprofit has only one chief financial officer, so most corporate workers who make the switch will land in the jobs below that one, at the pay those jobs offer.

The millennials who make the switch will mostly be the ones who can afford to earn less, as Clark, the former Apple manager, could after she moved to Wisconsin and took on consulting work. When nonprofits that are helping more people with fewer workers hire from the corporate world, those few millennials are who they'll get. Millennials without paid-off loans, a cheaper place to live, or a second income will keep trying out new work on the side while they hold on to corporate jobs they've already started to question.

#5478. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5477. Unrest in France looks like a ‘pretty big foreshadowing’ to economists nervously eyeing national debt at 126% of GDP

When U.S. markets watched as Paris metaphorically imploded just weeks ago, the consensus reaction was: “Let’s not do that.”

Unrest ripped through the French capital after protesters initially highlighted failings in the public school system. The action snowballed into widespread expressions of dissatisfaction with the cost of living and job prospects.

The macroeconomic health of the European nation is not in great shape: unemployment was 8.3% in Q2, real GDP growth was 0.4%, and wage growth was 1.7% at the national level. And underpinning it all is public debt, currently at 116% of GDP, with 30-year bonds topping 5.4% at the time of writing.

And the U.S. bond market, flirting with a wrap on the wrist for its own policymakers presiding over mounting debt, stalled. In fact, 10- and 30-year Treasury yields even declined.

“There’s a reason that the U.S. has pulled back a little bit in the last few weeks [and] why France has not,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told a Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) event last week. “It’s a couple of key indicators that differentiate us from France and suggest … that we still have a little bit of room to have these debates now, in the context of a K-shaped economy.

“We’re at about 100% debt-to-GDP; they’re at 120% debt-to-GDP. They are further along that crisis curve, and they are growing at about 0.5%. We’re growing at just over 2%. That’s a pretty big difference. ”

While economists largely agree that policymakers are perhaps naive in their hopes to simply grow the U.S. out of a debt crisis, starting from a point of strength rather than stagnation gives the economy a better chance of rebalancing its debt-to-GDP ratio.

But Long added that France also differs from the U.S. in that the former has exhausted much of its revenue-generating capacity through taxes. Per the OECD, the “tax wedge” (the difference between labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee) for French workers is 47.2%, according to its most recent data. The U.S., on the other hand, is down at 30%.

“It’s certainly not easy to raise taxation in the U.S., but from a financial world perspective and the bond market perspective, there’s a lot more room to experiment and to grow in the United States than there is in France,” Long added. “To me, the biggest warning sign from France is really not just the K-shaped economy effect, but the generational effect that’s going on and to see young people really driving this latest protest … from the disparities that they’re seeing generationally, and that seems like a pretty big foreshadowing [of] what we could see here as we creep towards 120% debt to GDP.”

As with any debt, the question of repayment isn’t if but when—and that’s the question budget experts are asking the public and politicians to think about.

Phil Swagel, the director of the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, said policymakers have a series of choices to make: How they might prepare for growth to slow if spending is cut, which forms of tax to explore, and so on.

“The other set of choices that you can think about with the deficit is about which generation is paying, so the longer we wait to make changes, that means some generations are … missing out on their share of the burden of the adjustment,” Swagel told the BPC event, “and then who within each generation will pay a tax.”

He explained: “The longer we wait means some generations, in some sense, don’t share in the burden of the adjustment. Then, who within each generation is affected? I think there’s a societal consensus it will be progressive, not in the political sense, but in the sense that households with relatively high lifetime incomes will have more of a share of the adjustment. But that’s a societal preference, and there’s lots of room for disagreement in there.”

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5476. A CEO gave his employees Fridays off. Three years later, revenue is up about 160%

In late 2022, Jake Kurtz, founder and CEO of Tampa-based social media agency Brick Media, wanted a better work-life balance. He had a wild idea: What if everyone worked just four days a week?

After seeing European companies experiment with shorter workweeks on social media, he launched a 90-day pilot in January 2023, giving employees Fridays off without cutting their salaries. By April, he had made the schedule permanent.

Nearly four years later, Brick’s revenue has grown dramatically. According to figures the company provided, revenue jumped 73% in 2023, another 39% in 2024, and 8% in 2025. Compounded, that’s roughly 160% growth in three years.

Kurtz believes some of that success traces back to the four-day workweek, though he doesn’t claim the schedule alone explains it. He bets that giving employees a reason to stay makes the company more efficient and more competitive, even as workplace researchers say the four-day week has faded from the hybrid-work conversation and some leaders who tried it have dialed it back.

At Brick, employees work four nine-hour days, Monday through Thursday. That’s a 36-hour week, four hours short of the traditional 40, with paid lunch breaks included. Employees are still considered full-time and eligible for benefits.

That puts Brick between a compressed 40-hour week and the 32-hour model some researchers advocate. At Fortune‘s Workplace Innovation Summit in May, University of Georgia psychology professor Malissa Clark argued that the point of a four-day week is to cut eight hours, not cram 40 hours into four days.

Brick’s schedule also contrasts with the long hours common in the related public relations field. Muck Rack’s State of PR 2026 report found that 55% of PR professionals surveyed had worked more than 40 hours the previous week.

Social media doesn’t exactly take weekends off, but Kurtz said clients have been surprisingly understanding of the arrangement, and most content shoots, meetings and other work can be planned ahead of time.

Employees still occasionally handle small tasks on Fridays or weekends, which he described as taking “five minutes here and there.” He estimated that more serious emergencies requiring several hours of work happen roughly once or twice a quarter. In those cases, nonexempt employees are eligible for overtime if they work more than 40 hours in a week, and the company brings in freelance contractors when needed.

The rule he goes by: Don’t bury employees in work.

Brick served 56 clients in all of 2022, compared with 85 in just the first half of 2026, according to Kurtz. A social media manager typically handles six or seven clients, with seven the upper limit.

Once employees approach that threshold, Brick hires more people instead of piling more work on existing staff. That’s one reason revenue has grown so quickly. It’s also why profit margins have stayed roughly unchanged since 2022, Kurtz said, as payroll has risen alongside revenue.

Employees also work from home most of the time. Only one of the four working days requires a trip to the office.

For Kurtz, keeping employees happy is as much a business strategy as a cultural one.

“If I can keep people here longer, and they like their job, and they’re communicating with similar people all the time, it just makes the business a lot more efficient,” he told Fortune.

Experienced employees don’t need everything spelled out. Kurtz said colleagues who have worked together for years can sometimes resolve something in a two-minute hallway conversation that might otherwise take 30 minutes.

He believes that efficiency translates into better client relationships and, ultimately, more business. Of the 20 new leads Brick received in October, 16 came from referrals, according to Kurtz.

The company’s resignation numbers suggest employees are increasingly willing to stay. Brick recorded six voluntary departures in 2022, before the schedule change, compared with two in 2023, two in 2024, three in 2025, and none so far in 2026, according to figures provided to Fortune. Its workforce has grown from 15 employees at the end of 2022 to 25 today.

Asked whether Brick could have achieved the same success with employees onsite five days a week and working frequent overtime, Kurtz said, “No, I really don’t… I think people would leave Brick Media for like a $5,000 raise.” He said he knows some employees have had better offers and chosen to stay.

“People have a hard time leaving the four-day schedule once they experience it, because they start to realize that life is way more than just the salary,” he said.

It’s the same case ThredUp CEO James Reinhart made on Clark’s panel at the Fortune summit, where he warned that companies sticking with five-day weeks will lose the competition for top talent.

For Andrea Echeverry, Brick’s director of client experience, who has been with the company since before the schedule change, switching to four days hasn’t meant doing less work.

“I think we have just found more ways to be more efficient with our time,” she told Fortune.

She doesn’t mind squeezing the same workload into four longer days. In fact, she prefers it. Echeverry said “hustle culture has played a role,” explaining that people her age are still willing to work long hours but take a different approach to the traditional “work hard, play hard” mentality.

She is a working mother whose husband also works full-time, and Fridays are now for spending time with her child and running personal errands.

To Echeverry, it’s part of a generational shift in attitudes toward work. Rather than accept traditional workplace arrangements simply because previous generations did, she believes younger workers are more willing to question the norm.

She isn’t alone in ranking balance over pay. In Randstad’s global Workmonitor 2026 survey, 46% of workers named work-life balance as their main reason for staying in their job, compared with 23% who cited competitive pay and benefits.

“We’re sort of like redefining work-life balance,” she said.

Kurtz doesn’t think every company needs to give employees Fridays off. Instead, he advises other CEOs to “think about what would make your employees want to work at your company.”

“I just think that there’s a happy middle ground where you can still have a really good life and a really good business,” he said. “And if you can also extend that to your employees, then it’s not only a feel-good thing for the culture; it’s actually a business advantage that your competitors won’t have.”

#5474. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

#5473. Apple Is Reportedly Slashing AI Budgets. Here’s Why Employees Are Worried.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Apple is cutting spending allowances for AI tools.

Even Apple, the most valuable company in the world with a market capitalization of $4.98 trillion, is watching its AI bill.

The tech giant is tightening internal spending limits as it looks to cut costs, Bloomberg reported this week. Apple is reducing how much employees can spend on AI tools to lower costs while simultaneously working to make the technology central to its business.

Some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending limits fall from $300 to $200 last month, per Bloomberg. The company is considering another reduction that could bring the allowance down to $100 a day for certain engineering groups.

Non-engineering teams also face steep cuts. Apple currently gives these organizations a $100 daily cap for AI use but is considering lowering the limit to as low as $25. Employees who need a higher budget to do their jobs can ask senior executives for an exception.

The spending limits apply to tokens, or the pieces of text and other data that AI models process to complete a request. Providers usually bill according to how many tokens employees use, with more sophisticated AI models typically carrying higher prices. Writing code or processing software can use a substantial amount of tokens.

Apple wants employees to rely more on AI but spend less doing so, according to Bloomberg. The company’s tighter budgets highlight the tension between controlling costs and using AI to overhaul engineering workflows and other internal processes.

The trend isn’t limited to Apple. Across the tech industry, the enthusiasm for letting employees freely experiment with AI is becoming overshadowed by closer oversight of its cost. Companies now have to decide where to cut spending without sacrificing the productivity improvements they hoped to achieve by using the tools.

Bloomberg reported that Apple employees are divided over the lower limits. Some said that the $300 daily budget was more than what most workers needed. Meanwhile, others worried that the cuts signal a wider effort to reduce spending that could eventually result in job cuts.

These concerns have grown as Apple brings in outside consultants to review how the company operates and where it could become more efficient. Bloomberg previously reported in late September that Apple’s new CEO John Ternus, who took over on September 1, wants a faster, leaner organization with fewer layers of management.

Apple’s bills are still climbing despite its internal push to cut costs. The company said this week that its research and development spending rose 32% in fiscal year 2026, reaching $45.8 billion. Higher infrastructure and AI expenses drove the growth.

Other tech giants are also watching their AI spending. In June, Uber limited all employees to $1,500 in monthly token spending. The same month, Meta said it planned to cut employee AI usage by adding token limits. One month later, Tesla informed staff that it would cap employee AI spending at $200 a week.

#5472. JP Morgan Athlete Center of Excellence: athletes need a financial playbook now more than ever

For years, the playbook was simple: athletes focused on their sport first, and financial planning came later. Only after signing a professional contract did they typically hire advisors, accountants and attorneys — and start thinking seriously about managing their wealth.

That timeline often no longer reflects reality. The sports industry has made tremendous strides in creating new ways for athletes to earn money. The next challenge is ensuring they have the knowledge and support to manage it.

Today, many athletes start earning meaningful income long before they turn professional. The College Sports Commission estimates that student-athletes received $1.77 billion in revenue-sharing pay in 2025-2026. Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) opportunities have accelerated that shift, giving student-athletes access to sponsorships and business opportunities while they’re still in school.

At the same time, the demand for financial guidance is growing. The 2022 NCAA Student-Athlete Well-Being Study found that many have a strong desire for more resources on financial literacy and taxes.

There is a big focus on creating more earning opportunities for athletes. We now need to put the same energy into helping athletes prepare for the financial responsibilities that come with them.

Too often, financial education starts after the money arrives. By then, habits have already formed and important decisions may have already been made.

The reality is that some of the most important financial choices for athletes happen before they sign a major contract. How do taxes work? How much should I save? How do I navigate money conversations with friends and family? Who should I trust?

These aren’t professional athlete questions. They’re life questions. And athletes are encountering them earlier than ever before.

One thing I’ve learned from conversations with athletes in my role at J.P. Morgan’s Athlete Center of Excellence is that they’re eager for this guidance.

I’ve spoken with current players who — when they were earning NIL income — budgeted for spending and invested the rest, only to find themselves short on cash when tax payments were due. They had the right pieces in place but only became fully engaged when there was a need to be. I’ve seen a lot of players learn to bring in their financial advisor this way — relying on the advisor to then quarterback communication among their agent, attorney and accountant.

Athletes should not be expected to be financial experts.

Just as athletes rely on coaches, trainers, nutritionists and medical professionals, they should be able to rely on trusted specialists for financial guidance. But athletes should also have basic financial knowledge so they can ask thoughtful questions, evaluate advice and make informed decisions.

I often encourage athletes to think of themselves as the CEO of their own business. You don’t have to master every function of the organization, but you should understand how the pieces fit together and remain engaged in the decisions that affect your future.

That mindset has become increasingly important as athletes build personal brands and create new income streams earlier in their careers. Today’s athletes aren’t just managing contracts. Many are navigating partnerships, content opportunities, business ventures and NIL deals at a young age.

The financial complexity has increased, and adequate preparation needs to increase with it.

The answer isn’t limiting opportunity for athletes. It’s building a stronger foundation of education and support around it.

First, we need to start earlier. Financial fundamentals should be introduced in high school, before athletes encounter significant earnings. By the time money arrives, the framework for managing it should already be in place.

Second, financial education cannot be a one-time conversation. Athletes’ needs evolve as they move from high school to college, turn professional and transition out of sports. The guidance they receive should evolve alongside them.

One of the reasons the JPMorganChase Athlete Council was created was to hear directly from athletes. This way, we can better understand the financial questions they’re facing and develop resources that reflect their real-world experiences, not our assumptions.

Athletic careers are unlike almost any other profession. Most people earn income over several decades. Athletes often earn a huge portion of their career income over a much shorter period of time. Opportunities can arrive unexpectedly, and they can disappear just as quickly.

If we want athletes to thrive not only during their playing careers but throughout the rest of their lives, we need to start with financial education long before the first major paycheck arrives.
