#5471. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5470. After Elizabeth Holmes Ate His Product, Everything Changed for His Business: ‘This Publicity, It’s in the Millions of Dollars’

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Ricky Hirsch, founder of Think Jerky, was “overwhelmed” when his brand appeared on screen.

On October 16, Ricky Hirsch’s meat snack startup Think Jerky experienced an unscripted marketing moment so crazy it’s “not even once in a lifetime,” the founder and CEO tells Entrepreneur.

Hirsch launched Think Jerky in 2015, building on his finance background and creative inclinations to start a “cool” jerky brand with a minimalist design and unique, chef-crafted flavors.

The brand’s sriracha honey flavor, created by Michelin-starred and two-time James Beard Award-winning chef Gale Gand, landed in the spotlight last month.

Hirsch was watching poker on television at his home in Austin, Texas, when he received a text from one of his employees.

She was in New York and had just attended a screening of You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 meta-documentary featuring Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the lead-up to her federal prison sentence.

Holmes was convicted of one count of conspiracy alongside three wire fraud charges stemming from more than $140 million in investor losses in 2022.

“ I was familiar with Elizabeth Holmes,” Hirsch says. “I’m in the business world, so that always intrigued me. And I saw the Hulu series. I was not familiar with Nathan Fielder at all.”

Hirsch’s employee was “freaking out” over Think Jerky’s cameo, the founder recalls.

In You Can See Everything, Holmes requests turkey jerky from the prison vending machine. The scene is reenacted with Amanda Seyfried, who plays Holmes in Hulu’s The Dropout. At one point, the camera pans to the vending machine — “it’s like product placement, the best, most beautiful shot,” Hirsch says.

The film ends with Holmes and her husband Billy Evans eating Think Jerky.

Hirsch decided to see the film for himself the next day, but he still had no idea how much the on-screen moment would change his business. “I brought some jerky with me,” Hirsch says. “And when it came on screen, I was overwhelmed. I was like, This is wild.”

The founder walked out of the theater in Austin with about 30 bags of jerky in tow. He started handing them out to people — and they “were freaking out.” It was a sign of things to come.

Within two weeks, Think Jerky’s honey sriracha sales were up 345% on the company’s website and 92% on Amazon. Someone posted on X that the Texas supermarket chain H-E-B had sold out of “the Elizabeth Holmes jerky.”

Reddit forums dissected what Think Jerky might represent as a narrative symbol. (“They think it symbolizes manipulation or control. There’s all these theories”). Fans dressed up as the Think Jerky bag for Halloween (“You have to make that costume”). YouTube videos discussed it. Restaurants reached out for collaborations. People hawked fake merchandise.

“If somebody wanted to pay for this publicity, it’s in the millions of dollars,” Hirsch says.

Hirsch chalks up some of the virality to how the brand’s name — “Think” Jerky — plays right into the “wild,” layered film and becomes its own sort of small character.

Now, the founder is determined to add as much fuel to the marketing fire as possible.

But that’s a tall order for a fully bootstrapped company with four employees. “People are stepping up, our significant others are stepping up and all that, but we are not a big business,” Hirsch says. “We do not have a big team. We never raised money, which is very unique in my industry.”

Hirsch acknowledges that people might not remember Think Jerky’s logo or company name in five years, but they might remember the shot of that bag. So he’s doing his best to make it a meme and keep the conversation going.

The team is going to San Diego for the Food & Wine festival. Gale Gand will make an egg dish (another humorous nod to the film) and top it with the jerky. The team is also planning lookalike contests, where they’ll hand out jerky and display a cutout of Holmes.

Sales remain strong, and Hirsch anticipates selling out. Think Jerky has about 60 days’ worth of finished inventory in reserve to meet the demand.

Currently, the brand is revamping its website, which will be complete in about a month, for a “soft rebrand” that fully captures the product’s chef-crafted approach. Think Jerky is also launching new products, including a Thanksgiving turkey stick made with four-time James Beard Award-winner Andrew Zimmern.

Looking ahead, Hirsch would be very interested in raising money for Think Jerky with the right partner. “ If Daniel Lubetzky wants to talk to me, I would love to talk to Daniel Lubetzky,” the founder says.

Hirsch is excited to continue leaning into Think Jerky’s surprise breakout and explosive growth.

“ I thought it was going fade maybe, after the third weekend, but it’s growing,” Hirsch says. “People are reaching out, people want to collaborate. I want to introduce my creative marketing and hopefully bring our company to a new level.”

#5469. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 3:00 amNovember 4, 2026 at 1:39 pm

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5468. You won’t be able to return a Christmas gift you bought on Amazon purchased before Nov. 1

Amazon, Costco, Target, Walmart and other retailers begin their holiday sales as early as October.

But there’s no need to rush to buy wool scarves, fuzzy throw blankets and the other holiday gifts on your list the second you spot some tinsel while shopping.

As a finance professor who studies how people and companies make financial decisions, I can explain why the holiday shopping season starts so early: It can help retailers attract more customers while allowing cash-strapped shoppers to stretch purchases out across multiple paychecks. And, for people with deeper pockets, buying gifts early can help them avoid the stress that goes with last-minute shopping.

Estimates for spending on holiday gifts, decor and the like between late 2026 and January 2027 range from about US$1 trillion to $1.7 trillion in the U.S.

Some 29% of Americans plan to shell out their share of those large sums in early to mid-December this holiday season, while 17% will shop on Black Friday, the day after Thanksgiving, according to the Bank of America Holiday Spending survey.

But many people like to shop for holiday gifts early – meaning before Halloween. Some do this out of necessity: They can’t afford to buy all the gifts they want to give unless they spread the cost over multiple paychecks.

For others, it’s more of a preference. In a 2025 survey, about 54% of early shoppers said they want to manage their budgets gradually. In addition, 41% said they buy gifts early to avoid the stress associated with last-minute shopping.

Retailers are adjusting by getting an early start on holiday sales and promoting seasonal items. By offering customers deals months before gift-giving commences, they can encourage even more people to join the early birds.

And by launching promotions in October, they might secure sales that otherwise would go to their competitors later in the season.

A longer selling season offers other advantages to retailers. It may ease pressure on their supply chain and logistics, since they can receive seasonal orders over three months instead of one or two. This minimizes shipping difficulties and lowers warehouse overhead costs.

Building more time into the calendar to move seasonal inventory gives retailers more opportunities to sell those items. However, an earlier shopping season does not necessarily increase consumer spending overall. Some purchases may simply shift from December to October.

To make sure that buying gifts long before the holidays occur is a wise move, early shoppers should read vendors’ fine print and research their return policies.

Many big retailers are making their return policies more restrictive by shortening the length of time you can return purchases and adding return/restocking fees.

In some cases, the deadline you face for returning an item could fall before the holidays. For example, Best Buy’s extended policy takes effect in 2026 only for purchases made on or after Oct. 30. Target similarly restricts its holiday-season returns window to items bought on or after Nov. 1.

Amazon extended its holiday return policy in 2026. If you buy an item from Nov. 1 to Dec. 31, it can be returned until Jan. 31, 2027, except for Apple products, which can be returned until Jan. 15. Anyone who bought gifts beforehand will likely be subject to a standard 30-day return policy, which will expire long before Christmas.

Shopping early is smart when the costs of waiting could outweigh the potential benefits of spending your money earlier than otherwise necessary.

For example, if a popular wool scarf that was priced at $100 in October is out of stock on Amazon by November, the supply is gone, but demand remains high. If you want to buy it for your mom and ensure it arrives in time, you may need to get it from other retailers. Maybe you can find the scarf on a website but is selling for $150. If time has run out, you might have to pay, say, $30 more for expedited shipping, bringing the total to $180. Clearly, you would have been better off buying it early on at a lower price.

But that doesn’t mean you necessarily need to rush to buy a gift weeks or months ahead of when you’ll be placing it under a tree. First make sure that the price is in line with your expectations and what you’re willing to shell out.

And you should do some comparison shopping to make sure other retailers aren’t charging less for the same or similar items.

Remember, waiting to do your holiday shopping until the last minute can lead to unnecessary costs, like rush shipping fees. The key is to have a budget, recognize when the price is right, and know when to stop shopping.

James Malm, Professor of Finance and Director of the Global Business Resource Center, College of Charleston

#5467. This Violinist Beat 350,000 Applicants to Become Snoop Dogg’s $10,000-a-Month Ice Cream Taster — Here’s How She Struck a Chord

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Concert violinist Annabelle Traves explains how she scored a $10,000-a-month gig tasting ice cream for Snoop Dogg’s company

How did Annabelle Traves land the sweetest job on the planet? Let’s just say she pulled some strings.

The concert violinist, who has soloed at Carnegie Hall and the Sydney Opera House, was just named Dr. Bombay’s first International Ice Cream Taster. In August, Snoop Dogg’s ice cream brand put out a call for the job, which pays $10,000 a month. More than 350,000 people from 130+ countries applied through HR and payroll platform Deel, which ran the search.

Traves, an Australian based in Dubai, starts a three-month contract helping Dr. Bombay expand into new markets, dream up new flavors and create a Deel-themed ice cream. Entrepreneur caught up with Traves to talk about her latest gig.

What did you submit to beat out all those other applicants?I decided to play to my strengths. Many of the other applicants owned dairy farms or had spent years researching dairy. I love ice cream, but I wouldn’t call myself a dairy expert, so I leaned on what I knew best. In my application video, I plucked a little of one of Snoop’s famous melodies on my violin. When I made the top 15, I doubled down with my own cover of “Young, Wild & Free.” I think that musical connection is part of what caught Snoop’s attention.

You’re already a very successful violinist. Why go after a gig like this?The timing was perfect. I had just come off a world tour with André Rieu, and for the first time in years I didn’t have a schedule that I had to coordinate a year in advance. Then there was the ice cream, and who doesn’t love ice cream? And of course, Snoop himself. I love all genres of music and have always loved his, so the chance to bond with him as a fellow musician was hugely appealing.

What do you look for when you’re tasting a new flavor?In one word, novelty. I want a flavor I’ve never tried before. Vanilla has been done a billion times. Dr. Maya, who develops the flavors at Dr. Bombay, introduced me to the idea that ice cream flavors develop over time. A couple of seconds in, a different flavor comes through. People talk about that with wine, but I’d never experienced such sophisticated flavors in ice cream until I tried Dr. Bombay. The nostalgia of the brand also stands out. Flavors like Sherbet take you right back as a 90s kid, and Peanut Butter Jelly Time does the same. I’d love to find flavors based on popular candies or afternoon snacks from those days.

#5466. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5465. FEMA’s maps undercount the U.S. flooding risk by about 6 million homes — and some of those maps are two decades old

If your home isn’t in a federally designated flood zone, flooding might seem like someone else’s problem. No one requires you to buy flood insurance, and the map suggests you’re in the clear. But reality may be very different.

Mounting evidence reveals that significantly more homes are at risk of flooding than is indicated by FEMA’s 100-year flood maps – about 6 million more, and 14.6 million properties in all, by one estimate. The official maps are commonly outdated, and some are two decades old. Even when updated, they typically rely on historical flood data rather than future risk projections.

But there’s another problem that redrawing the lines won’t solve.

FEMA’s flood maps answer only one question: Is the water likely to reach my neighborhood? They don’t assess an individual home’s risks or what the impacts are likely to be when the water rises.

To understand the impact, more comprehensive data is needed, including the probable flood depth at the home, the building’s age and construction quality, and insurance coverage.

When these other factors are considered, your home’s true flood risk is far more complex than the map might seem to indicate.

The data shows how two houses on the same street can face radically different risks from flooding, even when located in the same flood zone – and where local governments can help.

One home may be newer, well maintained and covered by flood insurance. Another may be decades older, at the low end of the same street where water runs deeper during a flood, and is in poor repair and uninsured. The same storm would leave them in very different predicaments, with very different paths to recovery.

Neighborhood averages can make it hard to tell which homes are likely to be hit hardest. But understanding an individual property’s risks matters for residents figuring out how to protect a home, and for local officials deciding where limited flood-protection money should go.

We study how flooding affects homes and the people who live in them. To see how much these house-by-house differences matter, we and colleagues Aaron Flores of Arizona State University and Sara Meerow of the University of Colorado Boulder built a detailed flood risk score for nearly 1 million homes in Houston. We describe the results in a new study published in the journal Applied Geography.

Our past research in Houston found that more than half of 100,000 documented flood-prone buildings in the city currently lie outside official flood boundaries, and that these overlooked buildings are more likely to be in poor condition and uninsured, leaving them especially exposed when the floodwaters do come.

The new research helps communities locate those homes.

To get a better understanding of each household’s vulnerability, we combined four types of information about each home.

We chose these four criteria because flood research consistently highlights their importance for how hard a flood hits a community: how much water arrives, how well the building holds up, whether people can still get around and how big the repair bill is for the owner. They aren’t the only possible measures; a city could use others within each category, depending on available data.

Homes in the same neighborhood can have very different flood vulnerability scores. In fact, we found the scores differed more from house to house within a neighborhood than from one neighborhood to the next.

In practice, this means that knowing a neighborhood’s flood risk doesn’t necessarily tell you how hard a flood could hit any individual home. A neighborhood could look safe on average while containing some of the county’s riskiest homes, and there may be many well-protected homes in an otherwise risky neighborhood. Much of the problem, we show, lies at the scale of buildings, not neighborhoods or ZIP codes.

Homeowners can check several of these risks themselves.

Ask longtime neighbors or your city’s flood plain office whether your home or the street has been flooded before. Look up the home’s age in local property records and have an inspector assess its condition. Find out whether the routes to work and school flood easily. And check whether you have a flood insurance policy, and what it covers: Most homeowner’s policies don’t cover flood damage.

Communities can apply our approach with their own data to locate particularly vulnerable housing where neighborhood averages may disguise the need for help. They can start with existing address-level flood scores, such as First Street’s, and add local records on buildings, roads and insurance. The extra details matter because officials have limited money for flood-proofing homes, improving drainage and helping families recover after floods. Better data on buildings and flood risk can help them invest wisely.

Data similar to that used for Houston exists across much of the United States, so other flood-prone cities could follow the same approach.

Floods don’t stop at the lines on a map, and they don’t hit every house on a street the same. We believe it’s time for residents and local flood authorities to prepare accordingly.

Yilei Yu, Senior Researcher and Postdoctoral Fellow in Geography, Rice University; Dylan Connor, Associate Professor of Geographical Sciences and Urban Planning, Arizona State University, and James R. Elliott, Professor of Sociology, Rice University

#5464. How I Built a Fully Remote Global Team Without Spending a Dollar on Job Ads or Recruiters

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Solopreneurs that provide digital services have a world of talent at their disposal. Here is how to leverage it.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Solopreneurship, despite its name, is anything but a solo pursuit. As we find success in our agency work, we inevitably need to build a team that can help us serve our clients and expand our footprint.

As MVRK, my CRM strategy and implementation consulting agency, starts its seventh fiscal year, I’m very happy to say that my team is now composed of seven individuals who operate from six different countries. What’s more, none of us live in the three countries where we mainly do business (USA, Canada and the UK).

I have hired each of the individuals who are on the team myself. And I discovered them in a unique but repeatable way. In this article, I’m going to review the method that I’ve used to build those relationships with potential talent and share how I’ve been able to make them a part of my team. All with zero dollars spent.

For the first three years of running my business, I operated fully solo. But as I started to build success, I had an important realization: The clients that enjoyed working with me did not want to leave.

One of the projects that I worked on in my early years was implementing an entire Salesforce CRM system from the ground up for a Philippines-based recruitment agency. This agency was staffing talent in North America, so I knew I had a connection I could leverage to find that initial team member.

I defined the requirements, and that recruitment agency put some talent in front of me. From there, I selected somebody who I felt was going to work. I believe that I got quite lucky with my first hire because that individual is still a member of my team.

While I support the recruitment agency model and believe it works for many companies, the reality is that an agency is still a middleman that does not add a tremendous amount of value.  In my case, eventually, the individual in question wanted to continue working with me, without having to go through the agency. As a result, we formed a relationship directly.

Of course, it’s important to check any terms of service that you’ve signed before you make this kind of transition. But using an agency is not the only option. There is a way that you can leverage remote talent without relying on the offshore recruiting industry. It’s a little bit more work, but it’s a lot more rewarding for both you and the talent that you hire.

As we come to the end of 2026 and move towards 2027, you need to realize that relying on talent only in your immediate geographic area is limiting your ability to grow. Except for industries where in-person presence is required for regulatory or delivery purposes, there is no reason why you should limit yourself to hiring people in your city, in your state or province, or in your country.

This world is big, and there’s talent to be found in a lot more places than just your backyard. The best way that I have found to discover that talent is to go to the online communities where they hang out, share their knowledge and build a network. Crucially, these are also the places where they can discover you without tremendous costs.

I have found Reddit in particular is an incredible source of talent. What’s more, I haven’t spent a single dollar on advertising job ads or on recruiter fees. I’ve been able to build those relationships myself. Reddit has various communities, many that are specifically niched to your industry, and it is those places where individuals from across the world are hanging out.

To find talent via Reddit communities, I’ve built simple intake forms asking the right questions to vet individuals. Forget about asking for resumes. Instead, my process is simple. I share a request for talent in a relevant community, ensuring I follow the rules of that community. Within that request, I ask people to fill in my form as a first step. This gives me everything I need to find individuals who look like the best potential options and invite them for an interview.

From here, I vet them using the standard process and offer extended initial term contracts to those who are a good fit. Extended initial term contracts are ideal in this situation. They allow you to extend the term if you find you work together effectively, but also provide a clean separation if things don’t work out.

As you can see, there’s no need to pay somebody else to find talent for you. For many solopreneurs, this is a waste of money and time. Instead, go to relevant online communities (Reddit is just one option) where those individuals hang out, build real relationships with them and hire the right people for your team. It’s a valuable route to solopreneur success.

Solopreneurship, despite its name, is anything but a solo pursuit. As we find success in our agency work, we inevitably need to build a team that can help us serve our clients and expand our footprint.

As MVRK, my CRM strategy and implementation consulting agency, starts its seventh fiscal year, I’m very happy to say that my team is now composed of seven individuals who operate from six different countries. What’s more, none of us live in the three countries where we mainly do business (USA, Canada and the UK).

I have hired each of the individuals who are on the team myself. And I discovered them in a unique but repeatable way. In this article, I’m going to review the method that I’ve used to build those relationships with potential talent and share how I’ve been able to make them a part of my team. All with zero dollars spent.

#5463. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5462. Coffee giant Dutch Bros made all of its executives, including the CEO, do a two-week bootcamp where they learned how to pour drinks and run stores

Dutch Bros CEO Christine Barone can do more than steer a $7.5 billion coffee chain—she can also hold her own behind the store counter. Like all other top leaders at the beverage giant, she embarked on a two-week bootcamp to learn the ropes of being a “broista.” And the chain’s workers weren’t afraid to call her out on mistakes.

“As I trained, people knew I was the CEO, and our teams would always point out when I was doing something wrong,” Barone tells Fortune. “That is one of the magical signs of a great culture that I need to make sure I build upon, because when my team cares so much about the customer that they’re going to tell the CEO that they were doing something wrong, I love that.”

The executive’s beverage training is part of the company’s “growth from within” model. Dutch Bros staffers, from store owners to senior managers, have been put through the course for years to understand the hard work of the chain’s 25,000 broistas churning out drinks. During the training, leaders complete six shifts of hands-on shop training, sharpening their hospitality skills, perfecting drink orders, and learning how to deliver on the values of speed, quality and service.

The chain says they witness first-hand how customer connections are made, and learn how to perfect drinks including the popular Golden Eagle coffee, so that everything tastes the same on Monday as it does on Wednesday. At the end, Dutch Bros leaders have to pass a “Flow” test, with questions ranging from drink recipes and company history to shop operations and culture. And the brand is serious about its standards; those who don’t pass have to retake the test.

Barone says the broista bootcamp reflects the vision of Dutch Bros’ founders: brothers Travis Boersma and the late Dane Boersma, who named the company in honor of their grandparents who immigrated from the Netherlands. Aside from gaining technical and hospitality expertise, she says the training nurtures “compelling futures” at the company, and lights a path for employees to work themselves up the chain of command.

“As we rolled it out to the more broader team across HQ, we were very thoughtful about making sure our marketing teams went through the training, especially the folks who are helping to design and make beverages,” the CEO explains. “Just thinking through: What are all those decisions we’re making that touch where the customer interaction is? And how do we ensure that everyone who is designing programs for our teams, or designing marketing programs, or designing new beverages, really understands what the shop environment feels like?”

After Starbucks and Dunkin’ Donuts, Dutch Bros is the third-largest coffee chain in the U.S. by sales and number of locations—and a huge hit among Gen Zers. But before ascending the caffeine mountaintop, the business was a humble roadside operation.

Their family dairy business was struggling, forcing the Boersma brothers to sell their cows and consider a new venture.

Their coffee business started off with a pushcart and 100 pounds of coffee beans back in 1992, with the brothers slinging espresso by the railroad tracks of Grants Pass, Oregon. Friends, relatives, and loyal customers kept their dream alive as the business grew. In 1994, their pushcart was upgraded to a drive-thru stand; and just two years later, they had expanded to six locations. The first Dutch Bros franchise opened for business in 2000.

The brand is known for its high-energy service and sugary drinks, which have since made their way to high school classrooms and office cubicles across the country. By 2018, it was already at 300 locations and employed 9,000 staffers, then private equity TSG Consumer Partners acquired a minority stake in Dutch Bros to grow it even more.

The years following were marked by major milestones, including going public, surpassing $1 billion in revenue, and beefing up its store count. Dutch Bros reported record-breaking revenue of $1.64 billion in 2025, up 27.9% year over year. And now, the brand boasts 37,000 systemwide employees and 1,273 Dutch Bros locations across 27 U.S. states. It hopes to grow its store footprint to 2,029 by 2029.

It can be difficult for businesses to preserve their home-grown culture as headcounts balloon, operations spread out, and outside investors get into the mix. One way to preserve it may be getting leaders to experience the business from the ground floor. The Dutch Bros CEO says that it has operators—a store or market leader responsible for running location operations—start off their career on the coffee line before moving up and into new markets. And as they advance into leadership and expand the number of locations they’re managing, they understand front-line issues and are skilled in building tight community connections.

“They’ll manage a region, so they’ll have their own set of shops that they’re managing. So why is that important?” Barone says. “Understanding this is the business that we’re in, and so when you have lived it yourself, your ability to understand where others on your team are starting from, you understand what that customer service feels like. That is important.”

Barone says that a “large number” of workers at HQ started off as broistas, enabling senior staffers to make decisions “through the right lenses.” That firsthand experience helps employees develop a sense of empathy that extends from the boardroom to the coffee counter—and serves them whether they stay at Dutch Bros, or choose to go elsewhere.

“When we’re great at hospitality, the definition for me is almost the ability to think through how someone else will experience something, more so than ourselves,” Barone says. “It really is great to be able to be empathetic…I think it’s a great skill if folks come up with us, or if they go and choose to do something else.”

Emma Burleigh is a reporter at Fortune, covering success, careers, entrepreneurship, and personal finance. Before joining the Success desk, she co-authored Fortune’s CHRO Daily newsletter, extensively covering the workplace and the future of jobs. Emma has also written for publications including the Observer and The China Project, publishing long-form stories on culture, entertainment, and geopolitics. She has a joint-master’s degree from New York University in Global Journalism and East Asian Studies.

#5461. Solana Validator Admission Ticket: Who Fell Short After Alpenglow, and How Marinade Responded

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

StakeThat +MEV went into one of Solana's first Alpenglow epochs with about 137,000 SOL staked with it and 0.8169 SOL in its vote account. The new admission ticket required 0.8198 SOL. It was 0.003 SOL short.

That's the first post-activation picture of Solana's Validator Admission Ticket. Most stake made it through without trouble, but a small group of validators keeps dropping in and out, often by amounts smaller than a typical transaction fee. At least one large stake program changed its delegation code hours before activation so its stake wouldn't stay with those validators. Marinade's published validator snapshots for epochs 1063 to 1067 show who fell short and what happened next.

According to Solana's BLS Pubkey and VAT page, Alpenglow has been active on mainnet since epoch 1064, which began around 13:36 UTC on October 21. From then on, each validator's vote account pays a 0.8 SOL Validator Admission Ticket at the start of every epoch. The fee is burned, and it pays for the following epoch. The first charge, at the start of epoch 1064, covered epoch 1065.

The rules are strict. If the fee can't be paid, Solana's page says, "your validator does not vote or produce blocks in the next epoch." Validators without a registered BLS key, or outside the top 2,000 by stake, are also excluded. Delegators to an excluded validator earn no inflation rewards for that epoch. The page also stresses that the balance "has to stay funded, not be funded once."

The vote account also has to stay above its rent-exempt minimum. In Marinade's data, the full requirement works out to 0.8197612 SOL.

Marinade publishes the inputs to its stake auction every epoch in a public pipeline repository. The input data checks whether each validator's vote account holds enough to cover the next epoch's ticket. Each snapshot covers about 670 validators and roughly 438 million SOL of stake.

Before activation, in the epoch 1063 snapshot, 33 validators holding 7.63 million SOL, or 1.74% of stake, were below the ticket balance. Once Alpenglow went live, that number fell quickly: 15 validators with 1.55 million SOL (0.35%) in epoch 1064, then 19 with 1.15 million (0.26%) in epoch 1065, the first epoch the ticket actually paid for. By epoch 1066 it was 13 validators with 790,000 SOL (0.18%), and by epoch 1067 just 8 with 710,000 SOL (0.16%).

The epoch 1063 count matches a figure in Marinade's own code history. A commit on October 21 notes that its new gate "refuses the 33 validators with vat_eligible false" in the 1063 snapshot.

The biggest pre-activation gaps were fixed in time. An unnamed validator with 2.05 million SOL of stake, Temporal Emerald with 1.23 million and Bitget Wallet with 593,000 were all below the ticket balance in epoch 1063. All three had topped up by the next snapshot. Of the 33 flagged before activation, 25 had recovered by epoch 1064.

So the fee didn't remove a large share of stake. The balance check affected less than 2% of stake at its peak, and about 0.16% by epoch 1067.

The validators that did fall short show a pattern: many of them nearly had enough.

Because the ticket is charged every epoch, a validator that tops up just enough to pass once will fail again an epoch later unless it adds more. Between epochs 1064 and 1067, between 3 and 11 validators fell below the threshold each epoch, while a similar number recovered.

The shortfalls also cut across setups. Every validator flagged in epoch 1067 runs either Agave 4.3.x, the client release the migration required, or the latest Firedancer build. Software readiness wasn't the issue. Keeping the balance funded was.

Solana offers a fix: routing block revenue to the vote account through solana vote-update-commission-collector. That keeps the account funded automatically, though the change takes two epochs to apply.

The bigger story is how stake programs reacted. Marinade, one of Solana's largest delegation programs, changed its auction code in pull request #153, merged at about 06:47 UTC on October 21, roughly seven hours before Alpenglow activated.

The change adds a new disqualifying condition, vatIneligible. A validator whose vat_eligible flag is false "gets no SAM and no backstop stake," because "Agave then pays its stakers no inflation rewards for the epoch." A null value never disqualifies a validator. The check currently tests only the SIMD-0357 balance, not BLS key registration.

The first version applied the rule only in Alpenglow epochs. Marinade's developers then caught a timing problem. Agave starts charging the ticket at the 1063-to-1064 boundary, and "a stake move made in epoch E takes effect in E+1," so the original rule "left Marinade stake on refused validators for epochs 1064 and 1065." The merged version refuses ineligible validators in every epoch.

The snapshots confirm it worked. In the epoch 1064 snapshot, 192,762 SOL of Marinade stake sat on ineligible validators, nearly all of it on one unnamed validator. By epoch 1065, that had dropped to 2,407 SOL, and by epoch 1066 to 10 SOL. A later commit gives the rule its own label and call to action in Marinade's interface, so operators can see why they've been excluded.

Marinade, in short, turned a protocol fee into a delegation rule of its own. A validator that misses one ticket loses an epoch of rewards, and it also loses Marinade stake until its balance recovers.

Before activation, Solana Compass reported that a community tracker flagged 45% of stake as not ready two days ahead of epoch 1064, mostly validators on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1. The following day, that had dropped to 20.3%.

Marinade's snapshots show the software gap closing much as those warnings suggested it needed to. Stake on Agave 4.3.0 and 4.3.1 fell from 6.56% in epoch 1063 to 0.08% by epoch 1067. Firedancer operators, who had to switch to Agave for the migration, dropped from 11.0% of stake to 5.9% in epoch 1064. They then came back strongly, reaching 17.2% by epoch 1067, well above their pre-migration share.

The large readiness gap was about software and keys, and it was mostly closed by the time it mattered. The fee gap was always small.

For most delegators, nothing changed: more than 99.8% of stake sits with validators that keep their tickets paid. For those delegated to the few that don't, the cost is clear: no inflation rewards for that epoch, and in Marinade's case, stake moved elsewhere.

The protocol sets one requirement: 0.8 SOL in the vote account every epoch. Stake programs are now adding their own rules on top, starting with Marinade's. Validators that keep running near the threshold will keep losing epochs of rewards, and possibly delegations, until they keep a buffer or automate funding.

#5460. Your Business May Be Invisible to AI. Here Are 7 Simple Fixes You Can Make This Week.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Learn how to improve AI visibility with seven practical website, content and credibility fixes that help customers discover and evaluate your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

Start with customer language, not marketing jargon. If you sell cybersecurity services to banks, someone may ask, “Who helps regional banks prepare for a security audit?” They are less likely to type your carefully crafted positioning statement. Your first job is to understand the questions that occur before a buying decision.

Write five to 10 realistic prompts from sales calls, customer emails and proposal requests. Include a category question, a problem question, a comparison question and one that names your market. Test them in more than one AI search experience. Record the date, precise wording, companies mentioned, cited sources and whether your own website is among those sources.

Keep branded prompts separate. “Tell me about Acme Consulting” checks brand recognition; “Which firms can improve manufacturing supply-chain forecasting?” investigates discovery by an unfamiliar buyer. Confusing the two creates false confidence.

Your 20-minute action: Create a spreadsheet with columns for prompt, platform, date, cited source, competitor and opportunity. Treat observations as directional research, not an audited visibility score. Repeat the same prompt set monthly to look for persistent patterns.

Too many homepages use language that could describe any company: “We unlock transformational growth through next-generation solutions.” It sounds sophisticated but leaves a buyer wondering what is actually for sale. If a customer cannot understand the offer in ten seconds, that is a messaging problem long before it becomes a technical SEO problem.

Replace abstraction with a simple structure: “We help [specific audience] solve [specific problem] through [specific product or service], so they can [realistic outcome].” For example: “We help multi-location clinics improve patient acquisition and appointment conversion through search, content and website optimization.”

Then add proof nearby: industries served, a concrete capability, a customer example or a documented credential. Do not paste an entire keyword list into your opening paragraph. Make the first 100 words accurate, readable and specific, with one primary H1 that matches the subject of the page.

Your 20-minute action: Ask someone outside your organization to read the first screen of your homepage. Can they explain whom you serve, what you deliver and what action to take next? If not, rewrite it before investing in additional content.

Businesses often publish broad thought leadership but hide the details a buyer needs: price ranges, implementation steps, eligibility, limitations and alternatives. That leaves both customers and answer-generating systems with incomplete information.

Ask sales and customer-service teams which questions recur immediately before someone books a meeting or requests a quote. Select five. Build accurate answers into the relevant service or product pages, not a disconnected wall of generic FAQs. Use a descriptive H2 question and answer it directly in the first sentence, followed by examples, constraints and the next decision a buyer needs to make.

If pricing varies, explain the variables rather than inventing a price. If delivery timelines depend on approvals, say so. If the product is not suitable for every customer, acknowledge that explicitly. Useful answers increase confidence because they reduce uncertainty, not because they repeat a search phrase.

This approach aligns with a broader shift toward commercially useful content. For additional perspective, Entrepreneur has covered how businesses can earn leads across both AI search and conventional Google discovery.

Your 45-minute action: Publish one complete answer on each of your top five revenue-driving pages. Review the result on mobile. Does a buyer get the information without opening an accordion, guessing terminology or scheduling a sales call?

“Trusted,” “innovative” and “industry-leading” are not proof. Any competitor can make the same claims. Instead, help a skeptical prospect verify what you say. That might mean a named subject-matter expert, clear methodology, customer references with consent, original observations, dated research, documented product features or a candid case study.

An effective case study explains the initial problem, what changed, how success was measured and what the outcome means. A claimed 300% improvement without a baseline is less persuasive than a transparent account of the metric, time period and relevant limitations. Not every business can disclose client names, but permissioned or anonymized evidence can still be useful if presented accurately.

For expertise-led services, include author credentials, an updated bio and an explanation of who is responsible for the advice. For regulated industries, prioritize accurate, appropriately reviewed content over speed.

Your 30-minute action: Select your most profitable service page and add one piece of verifiable evidence plus a short explanation of why it matters to the buyer. Then identify what proof is still missing.

You can write a perfect page and undermine it with a noindex directive, a broken canonical tag, restrictive robots rules or weak internal linking. Start by checking the pages that generate or could generate revenue. Avoid treating technical optimization as a giant sitewide project when a focused inspection of five pages will reveal practical priorities.

Use Google Search Console to inspect indexing and important search queries. Confirm that key page content is present as readable text, accessible from relevant navigation and consistent with its title and meta description. Structured data can support eligible search features when it accurately represents visible content, but no special schema guarantees inclusion in AI answers.

Google’s official guidance for generative AI search reinforces that strong SEO foundations and distinctive, useful content remain central. There is no requirement to purchase a special AI markup package.

If you want public pages eligible for inclusion in ChatGPT Search, examine bot-access policies too. OpenAI distinguishes its search crawler from other crawlers, so site owners should review the current documentation rather than assuming all AI bot traffic serves the same purpose.

Your 30-minute action: Inspect five commercially important URLs for index eligibility, broken links, visible text and relevant internal links. Assign each issue to a named owner with a completion date.

A website is necessary, but it is also a controlled channel. Buyers often validate a company through independent sources, including industry associations, credible media, customer reviews, professional directories and expert participation. Those sources are valuable because they can corroborate facts, not because a business purchased a large volume of mentions.

Start with accuracy: Is your business name consistent? Are leaders and services described correctly? Are your credentials up to date? Can a customer find substantive contributions rather than a directory entry alone? Then focus on places that matter in your market. A healthcare founder may benefit more from a recognized professional association or reputable sector publication than a generic syndication network.

Entrepreneur has also examined the role of credible outside recognition in a changing search environment. The practical lesson is to earn citations and mentions through work worth referencing rather than mechanically distributing the same press release everywhere.

Your 45-minute action: Correct three important third-party profiles, then identify one legitimate opportunity to contribute an original data point, expert explanation or customer insight to an industry publication.

It is tempting to turn AI visibility into a single number. But being named frequently does not guarantee revenue, and AI answers are inconsistent enough that screenshots are a weak stand-alone measurement system. Separate the signals you can observe from the outcomes your organization actually needs.

Track whether your brand appears for a consistent set of buyer questions. Record citations where platforms expose them. Review identifiable AI referral traffic in analytics, but recognize that some journeys will not carry an obvious referral label. Combine those indicators with form submissions, qualified meetings, pipeline and revenue. Ask new prospects how they discovered you, while understanding that self-reported attribution is imperfect.

For leadership reporting, a simple monthly scorecard beats a glossy dashboard that cannot explain its methodology. Show changes to priority pages, visible search and referral trends, sales opportunities and what you plan to test next. Make it clear which trends are observed, estimated or unavailable.

Your 30-minute action: Establish a baseline this month and choose one commercial metric to improve. A rise in citations may be encouraging; a rise in qualified opportunities is the outcome the business can use.

Do not confuse a seven-day implementation sprint with seven-day rankings. Search systems can take time to discover and process changes. Results depend on competition, platform behavior, website quality and the strength of your evidence. The point of the sprint is to eliminate obvious weaknesses and create a defensible plan.

AI search has changed the way some buyers research providers, but it has not removed the need for fundamentals. A clear offer, useful answers, accessible pages, credible evidence and disciplined measurement improve the experience for the human buyer first. They also give discovery systems more accurate material to work with.

The question for business owners is not, “How do I trick AI into recommending me?” It is, “Have I given customers and credible sources enough useful information to understand why my company belongs on the shortlist?” That is a much more productive place to begin.

For organizations that want to examine these issues more systematically, I use an AI visibility assessment approach through Bullzeye Media Marketing’s GEO practice. The same starting principle applies whether you work with an advisor or manage it internally: Diagnose the gaps before spending on execution.

Imagine a prospect asking an AI assistant to recommend a business in your category. Three competitors appear. Yours does not. You have a functioning website, years of experience and a steady stream of content. Yet the customer never learns you exist.

That scenario is worth investigating, but not because AI has a single secret ranking formula. Different tools generate different responses. Some retrieve live web pages; others depend on a combination of search results and existing knowledge. A recommendation can change with the question, location, timing and context. One test is not proof that your business is universally invisible.

The real opportunity is simpler. Make it easier for a person, a search engine and an AI-powered discovery tool to understand exactly what you offer, who benefits and what evidence supports your claims. You can begin with seven manageable improvements, many of which strengthen traditional search and conversions at the same time.

#5459. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5457. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

#5456. Tight Budget? This Familiar Destination Could Help You Cut Expenses.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

With less room in their budgets, people are turning to a familiar resource they may have overlooked.

Shoppers looking to cut costs are rediscovering an old favorite location in their neighborhoods: their local library.

According to a new report from NPR, consumers are returning to the library to get more without stretching their paychecks.

One avid reader, Izzy Rivera, picks up at least one book a week from local libraries near her residence in Topeka, Kansas. She said in an interview with NPR that it “just isn’t realistic” for her to regularly buy new books as she saves up for law school.

Rivera checks out both physical books and digital ones through the Libby library app. She isn’t ruling out buying books altogether. Last month, she went to her local library’s used book sale and bought 15 books for around $20.

There are other instances where the library provided Rivera with free or low-cost materials. For example, she watches movies on the streaming app Kanopy, which requires a library card or university login.

Her library card also provides her with free access to The New York Times online, a perk that extends beyond her neighborhood. For example, The New York Public Library began offering visitors free access to The New York Times in January if they accessed the digital newspaper while on the library’s Wi-Fi network.

Rivera said she spends a lot of time at her local library.

“It’s somewhere I can go where I’m not expected to spend money,” she said. “If I were to go to a coffee shop just to get out and do something, the expectation would be to buy a coffee, even though I probably didn’t want a coffee.”

Librarians and library-goers across the country told NPR that financial pressures are drawing consumers into libraries. The pattern is familiar to library staff: When money gets tight, demand for their services grows.

Americans are cutting spending on optional items as they try to afford the necessities. A Pew Research Center report released last month found that 44% of Americans struggled to afford at least one basic necessity, like medical care or housing, over the previous year.

Meanwhile, 70% said they had trimmed spending on nonessentials like dining out and streaming subscriptions across the same time period. Pew Research conducted the survey in late August, and about 5,000 Americans responded.

Several of the nation’s largest public library systems showed NPR data reflecting recent increases in membership. More library-goers are also borrowing materials and attending events.

Maria McCauley, president of the American Library Association, said in an interview with NPR that she attributes some of that growth to “heightened awareness” of what libraries offer.

Libraries “are especially popular right now, I think, because people are aware that everything that we provide is free or very low cost,” McCauley said.
